video_title: 🔧 The Wrench

summaries.summary: One morning, Bob rode his tricycle over a big rock on Ellie’s gravel. One wheel broke, so he needed a wrench. He searched his toolbox, tool shed, and workbench, but the wrench was not there. Bob went to Mega Mart to buy one. Mr. Mart showed him a fridge hat instead, so Bob bought it and forgot the wrench. His friends Pedro, Lucien, and Paulette said the hat was silly and reminded him about the wrench. Bob returned to Mega Mart, but Mr. Mart sold him musical pajamas. Again, Bob forgot the wrench. The next time, Mr. Mart sold him a screaming machine. Bob’s friends disliked the noise, and Paulette asked about the wrench. Bob then remembered he had spent all his money. He looked in the closet for more money, and everything fell on his head. Under the fridge hat, beside the musical pajamas and screaming machine, Bob found his wrench.

video_title: 👧🏻 The Three Silly Girls Grubb

summaries.summary: Three silly sisters—small, medium-sized, and biggest—walk across a bridge to go to school. Under the bridge lives Ugly Boy Bobby, who has never gone to school. He eats bugs, throws stones, and drinks from puddles. When the smallest sister skips across, Bobby asks who is on his bridge and says he will eat her lunch. She tells him that her bigger sister is coming and offers him six jelly doughnuts. Bobby lets her pass. The medium-sized sister then crosses the bridge. Bobby stops her too and demands her lunch. She says her biggest sister is coming and offers him a dozen jelly doughnuts, so he lets her go. The biggest sister crosses with two dozen jelly doughnuts. Bobby climbs onto the bridge and demands them. She says he may have them if he gives her kisses. Bobby agrees and changes from Ugly Boy Bobby into Robert. He goes to school, learns to count on his fingers, and sees tiny things under a microscope.

video_title: Sadie and the Snowman - Read Aloud - Little Golden Book

summaries.summary: One cold winter day, Sadie made a snowman with three snowballs. She used cookies for eyes, an apple for the nose, and a banana for the smile. Birds ate the cookies, a squirrel ate the apple, and a raccoon took the banana. Then the sun melted the snowman. Each time it snowed, Sadie made him again with new food decorations. The birds ate the eyes, the squirrel ate the noses, and the raccoon stole the smiles. When spring came, Sadie tried to protect the snowman with a blanket tent and then moved him under the porch, but he kept melting. When colder weather returned, she made him again with raisins, a peanut, and red licorice. At last, he melted into a bowl of water. Sadie poured the water into a plastic bag and froze it. When winter came again, she used the saved ice inside a new snowman and decorated him with cookies, an apple, and a banana.

video_title: Hänsel and Gretel (Fireside reading of the 1812 Brothers Grimm Tale)

summaries.summary: Hansel and Gretel lived with their poor woodcutter father and their mother near a forest. Their mother told their father to leave the children in the woods because there was not enough food. Hansel heard her and filled his pockets with white pebbles. The children followed their parents into the forest, and Hansel dropped pebbles along the path. When their parents left them, the moonlight helped them follow the pebbles home. Later, their mother made their father take them even deeper into the forest. This time, Hansel dropped bread crumbs, but birds ate them, so the children became lost. After three days, they found a house made of bread and cake. An evil witch lived there. She locked Hansel in a stable and planned to eat him. Gretel tricked the witch into the hot oven and saved her brother. The children found jewels, went home, and made their father rich. Their mother had died.

video_title: The Elves and The Shoemaker as recorded by the Brothers Grimm

summaries.summary: A poor shoemaker had only enough leather to make one pair of shoes. He cut the leather at night, prayed, and went to sleep. In the morning, the shoes were finished perfectly, though he had not made them. A shopper bought them for extra money, so the shoemaker bought leather for two pairs. The next morning, those shoes were finished too. This continued, and soon the shoemaker had enough money to become wealthy. Before Christmas, he and his wife stayed awake to find out who was helping. At midnight, two cute, naked little men came in and quickly made the shoes. The shoemaker’s wife made them shirts, coats, dublets, britches, and stockings, while the shoemaker made little shoes. They left the clothes on the table. The little men were happy, dressed themselves, and sang, “Aren’t we boys so fine and neat? Why should we make shoes for others feet?” Then they danced away and never returned. The shoemaker continued to prosper.

summaries.summary: In winter, the Ward family lived in a cold log cabin on the Ohio frontier. Wind came through the walls, and Joshua, Sarah, and William shivered in their worn clothes. Betsy Ward needed wool to make warm clothing. She had brought a spinning wheel, a loom, and a sock full of Connecticut coins to buy sheep. In spring, a herd passed the cabin, so Betsy bought eight dirty sheep from the drover. Josiah built a pen, but wolves killed two sheep. The family saved their wool. Later, one sheep ate poison weed and died, another drowned in a creek, and another broke its leg in a groundhog hole. Only one sheep remained. It had lambs, and those lambs later had more lambs. Season after season, Betsy’s flock grew. She spun wool during the day and wove cloth at night. At last, her children had warm wool clothes.

summaries.summary: Inuit call the polar bear nuk, or White Bear. It is made for the Frozen World. Its fat, hollow fur, black skin, small ears, and furry feet help it stay warm in temperatures below -40°F. It sleeps in snow, cleans its fur, and stays hidden against the ice. The polar bear is a powerful hunter. It swims far, runs fast, and catches seals at breathing holes in the sea ice. In summer, when the ice melts, it eats fish, birds, berries, and grass. A mother bear raises her tiny cubs in a snow den and protects and feeds them for two years, until they can hunt alone. Polar bears usually live alone, but two may play-fight before going separate ways. Inuit learned ways to live in the Arctic by watching polar bears. Polar bears are protected, but global warming is melting their sea ice. Turning off unused lights, walking, and biking can help protect their home.

video_title: Ruby Bridges Goes to School - My True Story - Words

summaries.summary: Long ago, Black and white people were kept apart. This was called segregation. Black children and white children could not always attend the same schools. Ruby Bridges went to a school for Black children, but the William Franz Elementary School was closer to her home. In 1961, the government allowed Ruby to attend Franz school. Her mother and Marshalls took her there to keep her safe. Some people yelled at Ruby and told her to leave. Parents took their children away, so Ruby was alone with her teacher, Mrs. Henry. Ruby learned math and reading, but she wished for classmates. After many months, children slowly returned to school, and Ruby was happy to have friends. Later, people wrote about Ruby’s bravery. John Steinbeck wrote about her, Eleanor Roosevelt sent her a letter, and Norman Rockwell painted her picture. As an adult, Ruby reunited with Mrs. Henry. Now children of all races can attend the same schools, and Ruby tells children to be kind and be friends.

summaries.summary: Sarah Hale was a writer and mother who loved Thanksgiving. Long ago, people in New England celebrated it, but many other states ignored it. Sarah feared the holiday would disappear, so she used her pen. She wrote thousands of letters to politicians and articles asking people to help. Women across America also wrote letters. States began making Thanksgiving a holiday, but Sarah wanted everyone to celebrate on the same day. She wrote to Presidents Zachary Taylor, Millard Fillmore, Franklin Pierce, and James Buchanan, but each said no. During the Civil War, the country was divided, and Thanksgiving became even less certain. Sarah then wrote to President Abraham Lincoln. She explained that a shared holiday could help bring Americans together. Lincoln agreed. In 1863, he made Thanksgiving a national holiday. Sarah had worked for 38 years, using her pen, and Thanksgiving was saved for everyone.

Their team grew and attracted attention, but World War II stopped the Olympic Games. The athletes then helped answer their country’s call. At the starting signal, Bill dived into the water and swam with speed, rhythm, and strength. He won Olympic gold medals, and people cheered as the anthem played. Sakamoto wiped away a tear. The Sakamoto Swim Club became an inspiration to athletes around the world.

video_title: The Floating Field: How a Group of Thai Boys Built Their Own Soccer Field (Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: Pret Hemman lived in a village built on stilts. He helped his father load the Longboat, but Pret dreamed about soccer. After school, he and his friends played on a sandbar until the rising tide covered it. While watching the World Cup at Uncle’s coffee shop, the boys decided to make their own field. They collected wood, barrels, and styrofoam, then built a floating field with fish neck goals. At first, villagers thought they were crazy, but later they stopped to watch and cheer. When the boys heard about a mainland tournament, their families gave them matching jerseys, shorts, and cleats. The Py football club won several games and reached the semifinals. Heavy rain flooded the grass field, so the boys removed their shoes and played barefoot, as they did on their floating field. They scored twice but lost by one goal. They came in third place and returned home happily, ready to keep playing on their floating field.

video_title: Love in the Library (@LiterallyCultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: Tama lives in Minoka, a prison camp for Japanese Americans. She does not like the desert, the fences, or the guards, but she works in the library because she loves books. The camp is very hot in summer, very cold in winter, and crowded. Every day, George waits at the library door with books to return. George is cheerful, but Tama feels scared, sad, lonely, and confused. One day, she cannot find one word to describe all her feelings. George tells her the word is “human.” Tama feels less alone and smiles at him. She learns that George keeps coming to the library not only for books, but because he cares about her. Later, Tama and George get married, and their first son is born in Minoka. They love their family and hope for a better future. Tama writes that the miracle is in people who keep believing in change, beauty, and hope.

video_title: A Bowl Full of Peace: A True Story (@LiterallyCultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: Sao lives in Nagasaki with her parents, brothers Aki and Ichiro, sister Misa, and little Toshi. Her family has a precious grandmother’s bowl, passed from mother to daughter. Before meals, they press their hands together and say, “Itadakimasu.” As World War II comes closer, food becomes scarce, school closes, and air raid sirens sound. On August 9, 1945, a bomb explodes over Nagasaki. Sao, her parents, Aki, Ichiro, and Misa survive, but Toshi dies. Aki and Ichiro later die from sickness caused by the bomb’s radiation. Sao, Misa, and their parents also become ill. Two years later, Sao’s father finds the bowl in the rubble, without a chip or crack. Each August 9, the family fills it with ice to remember those who suffered and died. Misa, her father, and her mother later die. Sao cares for the bowl and tells children, “What happened to me must never happen to you.”

video_title: Nian: The Chinese New Year Dragon (Literally Cultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: May hated spring because Nean, a fierce dragon, came from his mountain under the sea to eat villagers, animals, and crops. The Magical Warrior visited May in a dream and told her that she had 15 days to defeat Nean. The Warrior gave her a magical cane because May was born in the year of the golden dragon. When Nean came, May banged a cooking pot with the cane. The villagers made loud noises, so Nean fled for five days. When he returned, May used her red robe, bright lanterns, and a red flag to frighten him away again. The Warrior warned May that she had only five days left. May filled scarecrows with food and hid the cane inside her own scarecrow. Nean chomped the scarecrows, but he choked on the cane. It changed into a leash, and the Warrior captured him. The Warrior and Nean became a stone statue. The villagers celebrated, and every spring they used noise, red clothes, and lanterns to remember May.

video_title: 🦁 The Lion and the Mouse 🐀 Aesop's Fable Short Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: One morning, a playful mouse ran across a lion’s face while he slept in his den. The lion caught the mouse under his huge paw. The frightened mouse begged to be spared and promised that he would repay the lion’s kindness someday. The lion laughed because he did not believe such a tiny animal could help him, but he was not cruel, so he released the mouse. The mouse thanked him and said he would be nearby if needed. Later, poachers trapped the lion in a jungle net. He fought with his teeth and claws, but the ropes only tightened, and he became exhausted. Hearing the lion’s roar, the mouse came running. He climbed across the lion’s face and said the job was the right size for him. Then he gnawed through the ropes with his sharp teeth. The lion escaped and gave a thankful roar. The mouse quietly replied, “Any time!”

video_title: 🦋Pebbles And The Biggest Number Ep.4 - 🐸🌳🐠 In this episode you will learn about tree frogs and trees

summaries.summary: Pebbles crawled out from under a leaf and opened his wings. He met a tree frog and asked, “What’s the biggest number you know?” The frog said 3 trillion, the number of trees on Earth. Pebbles learned that a tree frog can jump 20 times the length of its body. He also learned that the oldest living tree, a bristlecone pine in California, is more than 4,800 years old. Pebbles asked the frog a question about the frog’s jump and the tree’s age. The frog answered both questions correctly. Pebbles looked at the rainforest and thought about its trillions of trees. Then a parrot said that about half a trillion birds live on Earth and called himself the most handsome. A fish said that trillions of fish swim in the ocean, then jumped back into the water. Pebbles also explained that rainforests get much more rain than deserts—up to 400 inches each year.

video_title: The World Is Not a Rectangle: A Portrait of Architect Zaha Hadid (@LiterallyCultured Read Aloud)

summaries.summary: Zaha Hadid grew up in Baghdad, Iraq. She watched rivers, green marshes, sand dunes, old cities, and ruins with her father. These shapes gave her ideas. She loved patterns, made clothes, moved furniture, and liked her mirror because it had no square corners. Zaha studied architecture in London. She filled notebooks with drawings and opened Studio Nine with friends. They worked day and night, but people said her swooping, flowing buildings were impossible to build. Zaha kept entering competitions. Her designs won, but a city committee refused to build them. Zaha did not stop. She designed buildings inspired by grasses, wind, shells, stones, stars, waves, and mountains. At last, her unusual designs became buildings around the world. More than 400 architects worked in her old school building. Zaha also designed chairs, shoes, a dollhouse, and other objects. She said, “You should do what you like,” and “I still believe in the impossible.” After she died, her architects continued her work.

She studied architecture in London, filled notebooks with unusual plans, and graduated with honors. Zaha opened Studio Nine in an old school building, where she and a few friends worked constantly. Her designs curved, swooped, and flowed instead of using ordinary rectangular shapes. Although judges and city committees repeatedly rejected her plans, saying they were impossible to build and objecting that she was Arab and a woman, Zaha continued entering competitions. Eventually, her designs became buildings around the world, including a stadium, opera house, bridge, museum, ski jump, and wooden building. More than 400 architects later worked with her. Zaha also designed furniture, shoes, and other objects. After she died, her architects continued developing her visions and keeping her work alive.

video_title: London: Alistair Understands Brexit

summaries.summary: Alistar is excited to join his school’s Elite cricket team, but the expensive fee and busy practices mean he may not play friendly games with his best friend, Manj. His parents, Jonathan and Lonnie, pay the fee, while Grandmother Rosemary proudly discusses Britain’s upcoming vote on leaving the European Union. Rosemary supports Brexit because she wants Britain to control its laws, money, and borders. Manj and his family support remaining because EU membership makes travel, trade, and cooperation easier. Alistar listens to both sides. When 52% of voters choose to leave, his history teacher, Mr. WS, leads a class debate. Alistar explains reasons for Brexit, but classmates call him a “Brexiter.” He is bullied at school and cricket practice, and his teammates stop letting him play. After talking with Mr. WS, Alistar leaves the Elite team and joins a new club team with Manj. His family cheers as he plays. Later, both families celebrate together, and Rosemary raises a toast to the UK.

video_title: Canada: Marcel Makes a Sacrifice

summaries.summary: Marcel lives in Toronto with his parents, Alin and Fran. He loves hockey, designs computer games, and is excited about starting a high school technology program. Marcel’s Uncle Jacques lives in the United States, and he and Alin often argued about health care after their father died of stomach cancer. Jacques believed American care could provide faster treatment, while Alin trusted Canada’s Universal Health Care system. Marcel researched both systems. He learned that American care costs more but has more specialists, machines, and private clinics, so patients can often get tests and surgery quickly. In Canada, people pay through taxes, but fewer doctors and machines can mean long waits. Then Alin was found to have a stomach tumor. Ontario scheduled his surgery five and a half months later. Marcel feared his father would get worse, so he gave up his place in the computer program. Uncle Jacques invited the family to the United States to arrange immediate treatment.

video_title: Flat Stanley at Bat by Jeff Brown |English stories for kids | learn English through stories

summaries.summary: Stanley Lambchop lived with his family. He was four feet tall, one foot wide, and half an inch thick because he had been flat ever since a bulletin board fell on him. Stanley practiced hard and made the baseball team as centerfielder. In the first game, the wind lifted him into the air, and he caught a ball that was flying toward the fence. Some people said the play was not fair, so Stanley asked Arthur how he could prove he was a good player for reasons besides being flat. In the next game, Stanley was no longer flat. His clothes were stretched and filled with socks and a blouse. He missed a fly ball and struck out. In the last inning, the game was tied. Stanley hit the ball and raced around the bases. He slid home just before the ball arrived, and the umpire called him safe. His family cheered, though his parents told him to wear fewer clothes next time.

video_title: Bedtime Stories: The Elves and the Shoemaker

summaries.summary: A poor Shoemaker has only enough leather to make one pair of shoes. He cuts the leather and leaves it on his workbench overnight. In the morning, he finds a perfect pair of shoes already made. A rich woman buys them, so he can buy food and more leather. The next morning, two pairs of shoes are ready, and a Merchant buys them. Each night, the number of finished shoes grows, and soon the Shoemaker and his wife become rich. They wonder who is helping them, so they hide in the shop one night. Two tiny elves in ragged clothes come in and make the shoes. To thank them, the Shoemaker makes tiny shoes, while his wife makes caps, clothes, and socks. On Christmas Eve, they leave the wrapped gifts on the workbench. The elves happily put on the new clothes and sing, “Oh what handsome boys we are, we will work on shoes no more.” The Shoemaker and his wife never see them again, but remain rich and happy.

He shouted that the pie was yummy for his tummy. Then he looked back and saw the shop disappear, leaving only purple fizzing light. Nearby, he found his purple bow tie.

He also said the carpenter would live a long life unless he died early. The carpenter went home, then returned with more questions. The room was empty, but the fortune-teller’s cap and crystal ball were there. The cloth merchant’s wife mistook the carpenter for a powerful prophet and asked him to tell fortunes. Using the fortune-teller’s words, he answered her family and the neighbors. People paid him, so he stopped carpentry. He became rich and famous, married the cloth merchant’s daughter, and lived happily. The real fortune-teller was carried away by a series of accidents and disappeared. video_title: Carrimebac, the Town That Walked by David Barclay Moore | Kids Read Aloud  Black History Storytime

summaries.summary: In Walkertown, Georgia, old Rotilla Redgums arrived with her nine-year-old grandson, Julius Jefferson. Julius found a thin white duck and named him Woodro, or Woody. Hungry villagers sometimes put Woody in a cooking pot, but he always disappeared and returned to Julius. Rotilla taught the Black townspeople to make rugs, jugs, and walking sticks that lasted in unusual ways. Their town began to prosper, but some white neighbors feared their work was magic. A man accused Julius of stealing Woody and returned with a torch-carrying mob. Rotilla and the townspeople faced them, and the torches changed into cornstalks. That night, Rotilla died at 100 and told Julius to carry her back to Africa. The next day, Julius carved a curved pole called a Carameck signpost. When the mob came again, Julius tied the post to Woody and told him to walk. The duck pulled the whole town to the ocean and across it. Lake Carameck remained where the town had stood.

video_title: When We Say Black Lives Matter by Maxine Beneba Clarke | Kids Read Aloud | Storytime for Children

summaries.summary: The speaker talks to a Black child about the words “Black Lives Matter.” The words say that Black people are wonderful and strong, deserve basic respect, and have been treated wrongly in history. When people call out the words, they walk together and raise many voices. When they scream and march, they say that enough is enough and things must change. When they sing and dance, they keep joy and courage despite fear. When they whisper, they remember terrible things from the past and the hurt they caused. They also see that trouble still exists and must be driven away. When they bellow, they say freedom is needed for all Black people who suffer. When they smile, they lift their spirits and say they are here, enough, beautiful, and brave. When they laugh, ancestors and drums help guide them. Knowing Black Lives Matter means knowing their worth. The speaker sees the child’s shine and says they will be all right.

They dance and sing in the streets, refusing to let fear destroy their joy. When they whisper, they remember terrible wrongs from the past and the trouble that still stalks Black people today. They say freedom is not complete until Black people have theirs, and they stand with those who still suffer. Smiling and laughing lifts their spirits. The ancestors guide them like thundering jambe drums. They know their worth, see Black children as radiant, precious, beautiful, and brave, and believe they will be all right.

video_title: J is for Juneteenth Children's Book | Kids Read Aloud Book | Black History Alphabet Storytime

summaries.summary: The story explains the meaning of Junth, a celebration of freedom. J stands for justice, which came when the Union Army arrived in Galveston, Texas, and told enslaved people that they were free. U stands for the Union Army, which shared the news of independence across Texas. The story says enslaved people did not learn about their freedom until two years after the Civil War ended, on June 19, 1865. E stands for equality, the promise of liberty and freedom. T stands for tell because Union soldiers were sent to tell the news, and the people rejoiced. E stands for emancipation, a freedom enslaved people dreamed about. Another E stands for excitement about the future of new generations. Enslaved people were strong and never gave up. Texas became the first state to make Junth a holiday. Junth is celebrated on June 19 each year across the United States.

video_title: I Am Harriet Tubman Ordinary People Change the World Read Aloud Video,  Questions and Activities

summaries.summary: Harriet Tubman grew up enslaved in Maryland. Enslaved people had to work without pay and could be sold away from their families. Harriet’s mother hid Harriet’s brother so he would not be sold. Harriet’s mother also told her Bible stories about Moses leading people to freedom. As a child, Harriet worked hard and learned about the North Star from her father. After an injury, she believed God was guiding her. When Harriet learned she might be sold, she escaped alone at night. She followed the North Star and used the Underground Railroad, a secret group of helpers, to reach Philadelphia. Harriet then returned to Maryland many times to rescue family members and other enslaved people. She later helped the North during the Civil War and fought against slavery. After the war, she helped poor, sick, and older African-Americans. Harriet said people should follow their own North Star and help others find freedom.

video_title: I Am Harriet Tubman Ordinary People Change the World Read Aloud Video,  Questions and Activities

summaries.summary: Harriet Tubman grew up enslaved, when Black families could be owned and sold. She lived in poor conditions and was forced to work as a child. Her mother protected Harriet’s younger brother from being sold, and stories about Moses taught Harriet about freedom. After a cruel beating injured her, Harriet believed God was guiding her. At about 22, she escaped alone from Maryland, traveling at night by following the North Star. Helpers on the Underground Railroad hid her in safe stations until she reached Philadelphia, where slavery was illegal. Harriet then returned to Maryland many times. She rescued about 70 people, including family members, using disguises, secret hiding places, and back roads. During the Civil War, she worked as a spy and led an armed raid, helping show that Black soldiers could serve bravely. After slavery ended, Harriet helped people in need and founded a home in Auburn, New York. She taught that freedom should be used to help others and that our own North Star can guide us toward the right choice.

summaries.summary: Harriet Tubman grew up enslaved, when Black families could be treated as property, forced to work without pay, and separated by sale. Her mother protected Harriet’s younger brother from being sold, and Bible stories about Moses taught Harriet about freedom. As a child, Harriet endured harsh work and punishment. At twelve, she became strong working outdoors and learned about the North Star from her father. After an overseer’s heavy weight injured her while she refused to stop an escaping man, Harriet believed God had a plan for her. At twenty-two, fearing she would be sold, she escaped alone, traveling by night along the Underground Railroad and following the North Star to Philadelphia. She returned to Maryland thirteen times, rescuing about seventy people, including family members, and leading some to Canada. During the Civil War, she spied for the North and led an armed raid. After slavery ended, she fought injustice and founded a home for poor, elderly, and sick African-Americans. She urged people to follow their own “North Star” and help others.

video_title: Words Set Me Free | Frederick Douglass Children's Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Frederick Bailey was born to Harriet Bailey, who walked many miles at night to visit him. After she died, Frederick lived with his grandmother, Betsy, and other enslaved children at Great House Farm. At age eight, he was sent to Baltimore to serve Hugh Auld and Sophia Auld. Sophia taught him the alphabet, but Hugh stopped the lessons because he believed reading would make Frederick want freedom. Frederick secretly practiced with chalk and a brick. He traded bread with white children so they would help him write, copied words from ships and newspapers, and learned words such as liberty, justice, freedom, and abolition. When he was fifteen, he returned to the plantation, but he was free in his thoughts. He taught Henry, John, Handy, and other enslaved people to read on Sundays. Later, Frederick and four friends planned to escape by boat and follow the North Star. He wrote a paper saying he could travel to Baltimore, hoping the words would help him reach freedom.

video_title: Lillian's Right to Vote Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Lillian is 100 years old and climbs a steep hill to vote on Election Day. As she climbs, she sees her family’s history. Her great-great-grandparents, Elijah and Sarah, were sold as slaves. Their son Edmund later worked in cotton fields and could not vote. After the Civil War, the 15th Amendment gave Black men the right to vote, but poll taxes and unfair tests stopped people like Grandpa Isaac and Uncle Levi. In 1920, the 19th Amendment gave women the right to vote. Lillian, her mother, and her father tried to register, but an angry mob chased them home and burned a cross on their lawn. In 1965, Jimmy Lee Jackson was killed during a peaceful protest. Marchers, including John Lewis and Martin Luther King Jr., walked from Selma to Montgomery for voting rights. President Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act. Lillian reaches the building, enters the voting booth, and votes.

video_title: 👧The Busy Life of Ernestine Buckmeister - Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Every morning, Ernestine’s father says, “Live life to the fullest!” and her mother says, “Make every moment count!” But Ernestine is too busy for her neighbor Hugo. She has a different lesson every day, including sculpting, water ballet, knitting, tuba, yodeling, karate, and yoga. Nanny O’Deer helps her follow the schedule, but Ernestine looks pale and tired. Ernestine watches Hugo play, and one day his ball lands in her tuba. She wishes she could play, too. The next day, she and Nanny skip yodeling and run to a hill. They look at clouds, pretend to be bugs, build a twig fort, and make a daisy crown. Ernestine’s parents search through all her lessons and finally find her laughing on the hill. Ernestine asks to stop some lessons. Her parents understand that she needs time to play. Afterward, they change their own routines, and Ernestine sometimes takes lessons, sometimes plays with Hugo, and sometimes just plays.

video_title: 🌊The Mess That We Made - Environmental Read Aloud - Ocean Pollution

summaries.summary: People make a mess in the ocean. Fish swim in the mess, and a seal eats the fish. A net catches the seal. A boat of welded steel dumps the net. The boat rocks in the current that swirls through the bay. A green and gray turtle rides the current, but plastic thrown away traps the turtle. The plastic comes from a landfill that grows each day and spills waste into the bay. The people at work and at play have filled the landfill. Then the people see the mess they made and act to save the day. They reduce waste and recycle plastic to make the landfill smaller. They rescue the green and gray turtle and haul garbage from the bay. They protest the boat of welded steel and collect the nets. At the end, they free the seal, and the fish swim in the ocean that they save.

video_title: 🗿🏝️Giant Island - Fantasy Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Ava, Mason, Cooper, and Grandpa travel by boat to Giant Island. Ava asks why it is called Giant Island. Grandpa says it has always had that name and that he visited to fish when he was young. Mason says the island is small, and Cooper says no giant can live there. They joke about giant fish and a tiny giant. Grandpa goes fishing while the children and Cooper explore. They find steps leading to a cave, creatures, shiny stones, and water full of secrets and surprises. They think magic is everywhere. They say no giant is there. Then Cooper barks loudly, and Ava realizes the whole island is a giant. Mason grins. Grandpa calls them back and says he caught no fish because something is disturbing them. The children say they know why: a huge giant wanted to play. They say goodbye and promise to return. Grandpa whispers that it is good to see his old friend. The giant hears him and grins.

video_title: 🐲🏴‍☠️Dragon and Captain - Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Dragon was hungry when he found a captain in his sandbox. The captain had lost his ship, so Dragon agreed to help. They went to Dragon’s cave and used a map, a compass, and a telescope to search. The map led them through a dark forest and toward the sea, but they found a waterfall and no ship. Dragon flew over the sea and saw two ships. One had white sails, and the other had black sails and a pirate flag. The captain thought pirates had taken his ship. Dragon and the captain made a plan to pretend to be pirates. The captain gave Dragon a pirate hat and used hooks to disguise them. They fooled the pirate guard, boarded the captain’s ship, and sailed away. Dragon blasted the pirate ship with fire so it could not follow. As they sailed, Dragon smelled meatballs from a castle and asked if the ship was faster than a sea monster.

summaries.summary: Ted is a giraffe and Unicorn is his unicorn friend. They love slime and bring sticky slime home, but Ted’s Mom says it is too messy for the house. They go into the woods to find a place to play. First, they help Mr. Egg, who keeps falling from a wall, by spreading slime on the wall so he stays safe. Next, they meet a sad little pig. They patch his hay house with slime and glue it to the ground. When the big bad wolf huffs and puffs, the house does not fall down. Then they help Mama monkey. Her children keep jumping on the bed and bumping their heads, so Ted and Unicorn put the last slime on the bed. The children stick to it and stop getting hurt. Mom gives them new slime and lets them play inside, but soon tells them to clean up the mess. The story says to be kind and not play with slime in the house.

summaries.summary: Darcy was upset when her best friend became sick, so she crumpled her play plans and went to bed. summaries.summary: Memorial Day is a holiday on the last Monday in May. People remember the US soldiers who fought and died in wars. People now go to parades and ceremonies, and sometimes have picnics. Since school is ending, Memorial Day can also feel like the start of summer. In the poem, children honor the day by raising the flag and letting its colors fly. They clap for soldiers because the soldiers fought so people could be free. A parade comes closer. Veterans march in lines with stamping boots, held-high heads, and shining medals. Then children think about summer, the pool, swimsuits, and splashing. They want to run and play, but first they honor brave soldiers and remember the lives they gave.

video_title: 🐲When A Dragon Moves In Again - Read Aloud

One day, the baby arrives. He looks like the child but is smaller, drooly, and noisy. The child and the dragon try to entertain him by bowling and playing airplane. Then the baby cries, so the child pats him, gives him a pacifier, and tries to help. The child remembers that babies like music. He wraps the baby in his dragon blanket and sings softly until the baby settles. The child decides the baby can stay until tomorrow.

video_title: 🤷Being Frank - Read Aloud - Being Honest Without Being Mean

summaries.summary: Frank always told the truth. He said Doy’s freckles looked like the Big Dipper and told Carol her singing was shrieky. He told Miss Aroma that her breath smelled funny, Principal Wiggins that his tie looked like a weasel, and his mother that she had wrinkles and was speeding. These people became upset, and Frank’s friends did not want to spend time with him. Frank visited Grandpa and said he was no longer sure honesty was best. Grandpa showed him how to tell the truth kindly. When Mrs. Peacock asked about her flower-covered hat, Grandpa named a flower he liked instead of criticizing the hat. Grandpa also honestly told Mr. Pickles that his relish needed more sugar and pepper. At the school carnival, Frank gave kind compliments to everyone. Carol invited him to ride the ferris wheel. Frank also wrote a kind poem for his mother. Later, Frank gave Mrs. Peacock a gentle answer about her new hat. He learned that honesty is best served with more sugar and less pepper.

Later, when Mrs. Peacock asked about her new hat, Frank said it was one of a kind. Frank learned that honesty is best served with more sugar and less pepper.

video_title: 🌋The Boy Who Ran Up A Volcano - An Inspiring True Story Read Aloud

summaries.summary: A boy loved to run. He ran over hills, through forests, across mountains, and over fields. Running made him feel strong, but other boys said he was too short and small to be a real Runner. When he grew older, he traveled the world and came to Aripa, a city in Peru. Huge volcanoes stood around the city. The biggest was Elti, which looked like a great Guardian. The boy decided to run to its top. In the cold morning, he began. He ran across sand and climbed the volcano. His legs hurt, his body ached, and the path became very steep. When the peak seemed far away again, he cried that the other boys were right. Then he looked down and saw how far he had come. He stood up and took one step at a time. At last, he reached the highest Crest. He felt proud. Though he was short and small, he was a real Runner.

Grandma hugged Samsoon and explained that farewells are natural, like clouds saying hello and goodbye as they move. Then Grandma and Samsoon went to the beach.

In autumn, Sam Soon and Mimi rode Grandma’s scooter to their favorite beach, and in winter, Grandma baked chestnuts, sweet potatoes, dumplings, and spicy rice cakes. One spring afternoon, Sam Soon came home from school and could not find Mimi. Grandma explained that Mimi had returned to her family. While cleaning, Sam Soon found a drawing of Mimi and Grandma and Mimi’s blanket, which made Sam Soon miss her. That night, Sam Soon dreamed of collecting stones with Mimi at the beach. The next day, while Grandma prepared Korean sushi, Sam Soon drew family memories. Sam Soon asked when she would see Mimi again. Grandma said farewells are natural and compared them to clouds moving past plants, trees, and birds. Then they went to the beach together.

video_title: 🌊🐄Mary Manatee A Tale of Sea Cows - Suzanne Tate's Nature Series - Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Mary Manatee was a huge, gentle sea cow who weighed over 1,000 pounds. She ate many floating plants with her bristly lips. Mary moved slowly, used her round tail to swim, and came up for air. She had a baby named Mikey, who weighed 65 pounds. Mikey stayed close to Mary because she taught him how to live and when to come up for air. They often called to each other with squeaks, squeals, and chirps. Mary worried about boats because their propellers could hurt Mikey. One day, Mikey followed a boat carrying a little girl. The girl called him “Hairy Mouth Harry,” and Mikey liked his new friend. Mary called him back, so he returned. Later, Mikey followed another boat through an open canal gate. The gate closed, trapping him away from Mary. They squealed for each other. Helpful humans heard them and opened the gate. Mikey swam back, and mother and calf safely swam away together.

summaries.summary: Salty seagull was the oldest gull on Little Island. His wings were droopy, but he was wise about the water. Cindy and Simon Siegel respected him, while some other gulls called his ideas bird-brained. One summer, a hurricane hit the island. Salty told the gulls to stay low and still because the wind would stop during the eye of the storm. The sassy gulls ignored him and were tossed by the wind. When the sky became sunny, Salty warned that the storm would return, so the gulls went back to safety. The storm soon came back and then ended. Later, cold weather brought fewer fish, and the gulls became hungry. Salty showed them how to drop clams onto a road so the shells would break. Cars made the road dangerous, so he suggested dropping clams on a new parking lot instead. The gulls listened to Salty, found enough food, and stopped being sassy to him.

summaries.summary: Abraham Lincoln, called Abe, was born in a Kentucky log cabin in 1809. He moved with his family to Knob Creek and then to Indiana. Abe watched travelers, learned his letters and numbers, and loved books. At home, his mother told Bible stories and his father told jokes. After his mother died from milk sickness, his father married a kind woman who helped Abe return to school. Abe worked hard, splitting rails, digging wells, and chopping trees, but he read whenever he could. Once, he paid for a wet book by working in a friend’s field. At nineteen, he saw Black people being sold at an auction block and knew it was not just. In Salem, Illinois, he worked in a store, became friends with Jack Armstrong, and studied law. He became a lawyer and then a politician. Abraham Lincoln was elected the 16th president. He used words to speak against wrongs.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Hanna's Cold Winter Written by Trish Marx, Illustrated by Barbara Knutson

summaries.summary: When the narrator was a child, Sundays were special. Papa, who worked at a paprika mill, took the children around Budapest. They visited bridges, baths, markets, and sometimes the zoo. Everyone loved Hannah, the hungry hippopotamus who quickly swallowed huge mouthfuls of hay. Then war came, soldiers filled the town, and winter froze the river. Food became scarce for people and animals, so the family stayed home. Papa learned that the zoo’s hippos were starving. He and Mama made a plan and took the children to the zoo. The hippos were cold and weak. Papa offered one an old straw doormat, but it did not eat it. He broke the mat into pieces and put them on a pitchfork. The hippo opened its mouth and swallowed the straw. After that, a cart traveled through Buda and Pest collecting old straw hats, mats, and slippers. People gave 9,000 items, which helped keep the hippos alive until spring, when the war ended.

The vine spreads through the broken fence into Mrs. Berman’s, Mrs. Brown’s, and Miss Pitcher’s yards, and across the road. When Mr. Miser rushes to pull it back, he crashes into Mr. Snoop Staggle’s bicycle and hurts his foot. The neighbors care for him, while the vine grows pumpkins in their yards. Mr. Miser secretly tries to take the pumpkins, but the neighbors harvest them first. He uses his pumpkins to make pies, but every pie fails. Crying, he tells the neighbors he wanted a pumpkin pie. They promise pies if he fixes his house, fence, and cat. The neighbors help him, and Mr. Miser becomes kind and thankful.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Mr. Hermit Miser and the Neighborly Pumpkin by Christine Noble Govan

summaries.summary: Mr. Hermit Miser lives in a shabby house at the end of Gilly Green Lane. His windows are stuffed with rags, his yard is full of weeds, and his thin cat is poorly cared for. One spring, a pumpkin vine begins growing in his lawn. Miser lets it grow because it covers the weeds and may produce pumpkin pie. The vine spreads through his broken fence into Mrs. Berman’s, Mrs. Brown’s, and Miss Pitcher’s yards, then across the road. While Miser tries to pull it back, he crashes into Mr. Snoop Staggle’s bicycle and injures his foot. The neighbors care for him, while the vine produces pumpkins everywhere except his yard. Miser secretly tries to steal them, but the neighbors harvest them first. He takes three pumpkins and spends seven and a half days trying, unsuccessfully, to make pies. The neighbors help him repair and clean his home, care for his cat, and make pies. Miser promises to change, and paints his house yellow with green shutters.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Mr. Hermit Miser and the Neighborly Pumpkin by Christine Noble Govan

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: From Sheep to Sweater by Robin Nelson

summaries.summary: A farmer raises sheep and feeds them hay, grass, and grains every day. This food helps the sheep grow thick, healthy coats of wool. In spring, a person shears each sheep and removes its coat in one big piece called a fleece. The sheep will grow a new coat during summer. Workers sort the wool and remove pieces that are dark or dirty. They keep thick, light-colored wool. Next, they wash the wool many times to remove bugs, straw, and mud, then dry it. Workers or machines comb the wool to remove knots. This process is called carting, and it makes the wool soft. A spinning wheel twists the wool into long pieces of yarn. A worker dips the yarn into colored liquid, so it can become any color. Trucks take the yarn to stores, where shoppers buy it. A knitter uses two needles to make loops and knots and shape the yarn into a sweater. The sweater keeps me warm, just as the wool once kept a sheep warm.

The yarn is dyed in colored liquid. Trucks take it to stores, where a girl buys blue yarn. A knitter uses two needles to make loops and knots, shaping the yarn into a sweater. The narrator wears it, and wool that once warmed a sheep now warms the narrator.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: The Biggest (and Best) Flag That Ever Flew, Rebecca C. Jones and Charles Geer

summaries.summary: Caroline Estefania Pickersgill lived with her mother and grandmother in Baltimore. Her mother made flags for ships. Soldiers from Fort McHenry asked Mrs. Pickersgill to sew a very large American flag so people could see that Baltimore was safe. Caroline and her mother worked every night. They sewed the red and white stripes and white stars in a large building because their house was too small. The finished flag was 30 feet wide, 42 feet long, and weighed 200 pounds. The soldiers raised it at Fort McHenry. Soon, British ships attacked the fort. Caroline and her mother watched from their attic, but rain and smoke hid the flag. The battle lasted all night. In the morning, the flag was still flying because the British had left. Francis Scott Key saw the flag and wrote a poem about it. The poem became “The Star-Spangled Banner,” America’s national anthem. The huge flag is now in a museum in Washington, D.C.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: The Mother Kangaroo By Edith Thacher Hurd Illustrated by Clement Hurd

summaries.summary: A mother kangaroo rested under a small tree while her eight-month-old joey stayed beside her. At night, a tiny new baby was born. It climbed into her pouch, drank milk, and stayed there as it grew. The mother and her joey went to a billabong with a mob of kangaroos. When a big red kangaroo warned that dingoes were coming, the mob ran away quickly and stayed safe. At two months, the baby’s legs grew strong. At five months, it had brown fur, opened its eyes, and began hopping outside the pouch. The older joey left to find a mob of his own. The new little joey followed its mother and hid in her pouch when danger came. One night, it became lost and called for her. At last, he heard and smelled his mother, and she came back. He stayed with her until he was eight months old, then later left. The mother kangaroo continued having many babies under the Australian sky.

At one year, he leaves her. The mother continues raising new babies under the Australian sky.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: The Mother Kangaroo By Edith Thacher Hurd Illustrated by Clement Hurd

The baby grew inside the pouch. At five months, it had fur, opened its eyes, and began hopping outside. The older joey eventually left to find another mob. video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Planting the Trees of Kenya - The Story of Wangari Maathai by Claire A Nivola

summaries.summary: Gary Maathai grew up in the green hills of Kenya, where sacred fig trees stood near clear streams full of frogs and eggs. She later studied biology at a college in America. After five years, she returned home and found the land changed. Many trees had been cut down for farms, the stream was dry and dirty, and people had little firewood, clean water, food, or milk. Gary told the women that people were part of the problem and could also be part of the solution. She taught them to collect seeds, prepare soil with manure, and care for seedlings. The work was hard, and many seedlings first died, but the women kept trying. They planted trees, vegetables, and fruit trees. The land became greener, families became healthier, and men joined them. Gary also gave seedlings to schools, prisoners, and soldiers. Over 30 years, 30 million trees were planted in Kenya.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Planting the Trees of Kenya - The Story of Wangari Maathai by Claire A Nivola

Without trees, the soil blew away, rain made the streams muddy, and people had little firewood, food, clean water, and milk. The women blamed the government, but Gary, also called Wangari, asked them to help solve the problem by planting trees. She taught them to collect seeds, prepare soil with manure, and care for seedlings. The work was difficult, and many seedlings died, but the women continued. Soon forests grew again, families became healthier, and men joined them. Gary gave seedlings to schools, prisons, and soldiers. Over 30 years, people planted 30 million trees in Kenya. The land was covered again with its dress of green.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Planting the Trees of Kenya - The Story of Wangari Maathai by Claire A Nivola

Wangari told the women that people were part of the problem, so they could become part of the solution. She taught them to collect seeds, prepare soil with manure, and care for seedlings. Although water was scarce and an early nursery failed, the women continued. They planted trees, restored forests and gardens, and improved their families’ health. Men, children, soldiers, and prisoners joined them. Over 30 years, 30 million trees were planted, helping clothe Kenya’s land in green again.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: From Wheat to Bread by Stacy Taus-Bolstad

summaries.summary: A farmer plants wheat seeds with a tractor. Sunlight and rain help the seeds grow. When the plants turn golden brown, the farmer uses a combine to cut them and take out the wheat kernels. Trucks carry the kernels to a factory. Machines clean and crush the kernels, then push them through a screen to make flour. The flour is put in bags. Some goes to stores for people to use at home. Some goes to bakeries. A baker puts flour, eggs, butter, and yeast into a mixer. The mixer stirs and kneads the dough. The yeast makes the dough rise into a puffy ball. The baker shapes the dough into loaves and puts them in a hot oven. The loaves bake until they are light brown. Then they are bread. The tiny wheat kernels have become bread, which people can eat as toast with jelly.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: From Wheat to Bread by Stacy Taus-Bolstad

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: From Wheat to Bread by Stacy Taus-Bolstad

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Come With Me by Holly M. McGee, Illustrated by Pascal Lemaitre

summaries.summary: A little girl is frightened by news of anger and hatred between people. She asks her papa how she can help make the world better. Papa says, “Come with me.” They hold hands, go to the subway, and ride the train through tunnels. Papa tips his hat to people, and the girl does too. They are brave and kind, and win a small battle over fear. Later, the girl asks her mama the same question. Mama says, “Come with me.” They buy food at the grocery, then Mama cooks while the girl sets the table. She eats with Mama and Papa, while her dog nuzzles her. She scratches him and asks to walk the dog. Her parents let her go to show they will not live in fear. A boy across the hall joins her. The girl says, “Come with me,” because two people are stronger than one. Together, they walk happily and choose to be brave, gentle, strong, and kind to all living things. The story says everyone’s small part matters.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: George Washington by David A. Adler illustrated by John & Alexandra Wallner

summaries.summary: George Washington was born in 1732 in a Virginia farmhouse. He enjoyed fishing, boating, and riding horses. He learned to read, write, and do arithmetic. After his father died, George helped his mother and cared for his younger brothers and sister. He found his father’s surveying tools and learned to measure land. At 16, he surveyed the Virginia wilderness. In 1753, he joined the Virginia army, and during the French and Indian War, he bravely led soldiers against the French. He married Martha Custis and lived at Mount Vernon. In 1775, the 13 colonies chose George to lead the Continental Army against England. After eight years, the colonies won and became states. In 1789, George became the first president of the United States and was elected again in 1792. He made treaties, kept the country out of a European war, and enforced the law during the whiskey attacks. In 1797, he returned to Mount Vernon. He died there in 1799.

After leaving office, he returned to Mount Vernon and watched a new capital city being built. It was named Washington. He died there in 1799.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: George Washington by David A. Adler illustrated by John & Alexandra Wallner

summaries.summary: George Washington was born on February 22, 1732, in a Virginia farmhouse. He enjoyed riding, boating, and fishing, and he learned reading, writing, and arithmetic. Despite shortages of food, clothing, and weapons, his army fought for eight years and won independence in 1783. The colonies formed the United States, and Washington became its first president in 1789. He was re-elected in 1792, made treaties, kept the country out of a European war, and enforced laws. He retired to Mount Vernon in 1797 and died there in 1799. He was called the Father of our country.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Animals Born Alive and Well by Ruth Heller

summaries.summary: Mammals are animals with fur or hair. They breathe fresh air, are born alive, and drink milk from their mothers. The spiny anteater and duckbill platypus are the only mammals that lay eggs. Mammals can have many coverings, including stripes, spots, scales, or spikes. Examples are elephants, zebras, tigers, giraffes, pangolins, armadillos, and porcupines. Marsupials, such as kangaroos and koalas, are born very small and grow in their mothers’ pouches. Other mammals live on land, fly like bats, climb like monkeys, or live in the sea. Sea mammals, such as dolphins, whales, seals, walruses, and manatees, must come up for air. Some have babies in the sea, while others leave the water. Prehistoric animals were mammals too. The blue whale is the largest mammal, and the shrew is the smallest. People are mammals. All animals born alive are viviparous. In winter, spring, summer, and fall, a snowshoe hare’s hair changes.

video_title: Kids Book Read Aloud: Animals Born Alive and Well by Ruth Heller

Mammals live on land, underground, in trees, and in the air, like bats. Sea mammals, including porpoises, whales, walruses, seals, manatees, dolphins, and sea otters, must come up for air. Some have babies in the sea, while others leave the water. Prehistoric animals were mammals too. The blue whale is the largest mammal, and the shrew is the smallest. People are mammals, and all animals born alive are viviparous. Hair changes with winter, spring, summer, and fall.

video_title: 🚀 I AM SUPERMAN - Read Aloud with Ms. Linda | Brightly Storytime

summaries.summary: Cal L was born on Krypton, a planet that was dying. His scientist father and his mother, Lara, sent him to Earth in a rocket so he would live. Jonathan and Martha Kent found the baby and adopted him. They named him Clark Kent. Clark was very strong and could do amazing things, but his parents taught him to be kind, work hard, respect others, and help people in danger. They also told him he was on Earth for a reason. Clark sometimes felt lonely because he was different. Near the end of high school, his father died, and Martha helped him find courage. Later, Clark learned he could fly, see through things, use heat vision and super breath, and survive almost anything. He became Superman and worked as a journalist at the Daily Planet in Metropolis. He kept his identity secret and helped people. Clark says his greatest strength comes from his heart and kindness, not only his powers.

video_title: 🚀 I AM SUPERMAN - Read Aloud with Ms. Linda | Brightly Storytime

Clark sometimes felt lonely because he was different, but his parents loved him and told him he was on Earth for a reason. After Pa died near the end of high school, Clark decided to discover that reason. He learned he could fly, use X-ray, heat, and super vision, leap over buildings, and withstand almost anything except magic and kryptonite. He became Superman and worked as a journalist at the Daily Planet while keeping his identity secret. Superman helps people, but he says his greatest strength comes from his heart and his parents’ lessons: kindness and being a good person can change the world.

video_title: 🚀 I AM SUPERMAN - Read Aloud with Ms. Linda | Brightly Storytime

video_title: The Station Cat - Read Aloud With The Author | Brightly Storytime

summaries.summary: A cold, gray railway station is home to a small, hungry cat with bright, colorful fur. She calls for her mother, but no one helps her. A conductor tells her she cannot board the 1422 train to Withersfield because she has no ticket. The cat stays at the station. She comforts a sad man who once wanted to paint, and he remembers his dream and stays with her instead of taking his train. She stops a lonely schoolboy from going into the dark woods. He pets her, feels happier, and goes to school. She also stops a grieving woman from taking a train to the coast. The woman cries, then laughs and returns to her usual train. The cat becomes loved by everyone, and the station grows bright and happy. The man displays paintings, the boy becomes station master, and the woman plants flowers. When the cat grows old, the conductor returns. She has earned her ticket and boards the train to the next station.

summaries.summary: Dragon stories come from many places, so dragons have different shapes and powers. Many can fly, have reptile or bird parts, long tails, and fiery or poisonous breath. In Asia, dragons are often wise and kind. China’s long has parts from many animals, controls water and weather, and brings good luck. Indian nagas are part human and part snake, while Indonesian nagas guard water, gates, and treasure. The Philippine Bakunawa can swallow the moon. Korean imugi bring luck, and Japan’s Ryujin rules the ocean. In Europe, dragons were once part of nature but later became dangerous enemies. The Welsh red dragon breathes fire, the wyvern hunts large animals, and the lindworm is a huge serpent. Around the world, Apep causes darkness, Aida Huedo helps create Earth, and Amaroo rises during earthquakes. Some real animals are also called dragons, including the Komodo dragon, flying dragon, sea dragon, and black dragon fish.

Then he made a hole, came out, and became a beautiful butterfly.

summaries.summary: The story explains that people should be quiet sometimes, but they should speak up when something important happens. If someone is hurt by words or fists, they should be an ally and tell others so the person can be safe. They can share time with someone who is lonely, say sorry after a mistake, and thank someone for a special day or gift. When they feel sad, they can ask for help. They should protect trees and creatures by bringing people together. They must tell a grown-up about a scary secret involving harm. They should also speak up when a group is choosing the wrong path. Even a quiet voice can make a difference.

Rosie explained its four layers, but they did not find orangutans. During rain, they sheltered under a banana tree and saw bugs recycling dead leaves and wood into soil. Next, they found a huge Rafflesia, or stinking corpse flower. Its smell attracted flies. They followed large footprints and photographed elephants cooling in the river. Then a tiger and her cubs passed nearby, so Max and Rosie hid. They climbed into the canopy and saw many monkeys, including one that checked Rosie's hair for fleas. At night, they saw fireflies and a flying fox, which was really a giant bat. In the morning, orangutans appeared. One cracked nuts with a rock while young orangutans played in the trees. Max took their photo before they swung away. Max and Rosie were happy to find them because orangutans are very rare.

Aladdin, a kind-hearted thief, helps Jasmine escape by distracting Jamal with his monkey, Abu. Jasmine and Aladdin flee across the rooftops and hide in Aladdin’s tower. He does not know she is a princess, but he admires her cleverness and caring heart. Jasmine studies books and maps because she wants to improve life for Agrabah’s people. Her father expects her to marry a prince, but Jasmine dislikes the suitors because they care only about her beauty and wealth. Her tiger, Raja, dislikes them too. Jasmine faces her father’s protectiveness and Jafar’s wish to control her. With Raja and her handmaiden Dahlia supporting her, Jasmine proves she is preparing to lead Agrabah. Her adventure is just beginning.

video_title: Mickey & Friends, Goofy at Bat Book

summaries.summary: Goofy decides to sign up for a new game because he knows his friends can teach him. He asks Donald to be his coach. Donald shows him how to hold the bat tightly. Mickey pitches a curving ball, and Goofy gets tangled up trying to hit it. Donald tells Goofy to hit the next ball far, but the pitch takes so long that Goofy falls asleep. Mickey throws another fast pitch. Goofy swings hard and sends the ball flying low. Donald tells him to run home, but then calls for him to run to third base instead. Later, Goofy uses a net while Minnie bats. Minnie hits the ball toward the seats, and Goofy runs quickly to catch it. Donald says Goofy can go far and become a star at the game. Donald tells Goofy that he should play too. Goofy asks Donald to try out, and says that Donald’s help brings him good luck. Donald agrees because playing is more fun with Goofy.

Anna finds the old book their parents read to them and some face cream. The sisters build a fort with pillows, blankets, icy tunnels, and snow turrets. Then they have a playful snowball fight. Olaf knocks on the door and joins the sleepover, though he does not know what a sleepover is. The friends play Pickup Sticks, draw and sculpt, and act out charades. Anna tells a scary story about the Harry Hooligan, and a low moan comes from outside. Elsa, Anna, and Olaf see a shadow and go to investigate. They discover Sven, who cannot sleep because Kristoff is snoring. Sven joins them. Later, Elsa reads the old book while everyone gets comfortable. Anna, Olaf, and Sven fall asleep, so Elsa tucks them in and goes to sleep too.

video_title: Disney's MOANA - The Complete Epic Adventure!

summaries.summary: At first, there was only the ocean. Then the beautiful island Te Fiti rose from the waves. Her heart had the power to create life, so she made birds, fish, plants, islands, and people. Everything lived in harmony. Some people wanted Te Fiti’s Heart because they thought its power could belong to them. Maui, a trickster demigod of the Wind and Sea, decided to steal it. With his magical fishhook, he traveled to Te Fiti and changed into a hawk, a lizard, and then a beetle to reach the Sacred Space. He became human, used his fishhook, and took the glowing heart. The island shook and began to crumble. Plants and trees died, and Darkness spread. Maui changed shapes to escape falling rocks and flew toward his boat. A lava demon of Earth and Fire named Take Ha attacked him. Maui tried to fight with his fishhook, but Take Ha knocked him from the sky. Maui was never seen again, and the Darkness kept spreading until Te Fiti’s heart could be restored.

Moana realizes she has been standing on Tamatoa’s back.

video_title: Giant Island - by Jane Yolen illustrated by Doug Keith | Read-Aloud

summaries.summary: Giant Island was small and low in the water when Ava, Mason, Grandpa, and Cooper arrived by boat. Ava asked why it had that name. Grandpa said it had always been called Giant Island and that he had fished there as a boy. Mason said no giant could live there. Grandpa guessed there might be giant fish, and Ava joked about a tiny giant. Grandpa began fishing while the children followed Cooper. Cooper found steps, and they explored a dripping cave. They saw creatures, shiny stones, and bubbling water. They searched but found no giant. Then Cooper barked loudly. Ava understood that the whole island looked like a giant with a grin. When Grandpa called them back, he said something had disturbed the fish. The children said a huge giant had wanted to play with them. They said goodbye and promised to return. Grandpa quietly greeted the island as an old friend, and the giant heard him and grinned.

video_title: Cendrillon - By Robert D. San Souci & Illustrated by Brian Pinkney | Read-Aloud

summaries.summary: A poor washerwoman named Nannin' lives on a green island in the Caribbean Sea. Her mother left her a magic mahogany wand. Three taps can change one thing into another for a short time, but the magic must help someone she loves. Nannin' loves her goddaughter, Cendrillon. Cendrillon works hard for her cruel stepmother, Madame Prospèrine, and her stepsister, Vitaline. She is not allowed to go to Paul Thibault's birthday ball. Nannin' uses the wand to make a coach, horses, servants, and a beautiful dress for Cendrillon. At the ball, Paul dances only with Cendrillon. Near midnight, they leave, but Cendrillon loses one pink slipper. The magic ends, and she becomes poor again. Paul finds the slipper and searches for its owner. It fits Cendrillon. Paul sees that he truly loves her, even without magic. They marry, and Nannin' joins the joyful wedding.

video_title: Henny Penny | Read-Along | 1970 Scholastic Record & Book | Vintage Children's Story

summaries.summary: Henny Penny was picking up corn in the farmyard when an acorn hit her head. She thought the sky was falling, so she decided to tell the king. On the way, she met Cocky Locky and invited him to come along. Then they met Ducky Lucky, Goosey Lucy, and Turkey Lurkey, and each joined the group to tell the king about the falling sky. Soon they met Foxy Loxy. He said they were not on the right road and offered to show them a shortcut to the king’s palace. Henny Penny and the others followed him. Foxy Loxy led them to his cave, and they all went inside after him. After that day, Henny Penny, Cocky Locky, Ducky Lucky, Goosey Lucy, and Turkey Lurkey were never seen again. The king was never told that the sky was falling. Foxy Loxy, Mrs. Foxy Loxy, and their seven little foxes remembered the feast they had that day.

Another day, Mudpie goes into the backyard to pick flowers for his mom. The bumblybees bother him, so he runs away and gets a band-aid. His mom does not get the flowers. Mudpie brings her another present, but it runs away too. His mom still says thank you because he tried to give her something. Mudpie says that his mom is OK in a thousand ways every day. The story ends with Mudpie showing his love by helping and giving gifts.

video_title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland Read Aloud (abridged) - Part One

summaries.summary: Alice sat by the river with her sister. She was hot, sleepy, and bored because the book had no pictures or conversations. Then a White Rabbit ran by, saying, “Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be too late!” The Rabbit looked at a watch and jumped into a rabbit hole. Alice followed and fell down a very deep well. She passed cupboards and bookshelves on the walls before landing safely on sticks and dry leaves. Alice chased the Rabbit through a tunnel, but he disappeared. She entered a long hall with many locked doors. A tiny golden key on a glass table opened a little door. Through it, Alice saw a beautiful garden, but the door was too small for her. She returned to the table and found a bottle labeled “DRINK ME.” It was not marked Poison, so Alice tasted it. It tasted like many different foods, and she drank it all.

Sarah’s father shows them pictures of fighting, accidents, and people being unkind. He reads letters from the Lambchops. Stanley asks for clothes and tents for people who lost their homes in an earthquake. Arthur asks for food and little stoves. Their parents write that they believe in Santa. Sarah’s father thinks the family tricked him because Stanley is no longer flat. Stanley remembers a photograph of himself flat under a door. The picture proves his letter was true, so Sarah’s father agrees to deliver the gifts. The Lambchops return home. On Christmas, news shows the earthquake survivors receiving the clothes, tents, food, stoves, and chocolate bars.

summaries.summary: Milly Bogan travels with her husband, Forbes, along the A 406. She is bored, so she plays a game at traffic lights. She tells drivers, “Please help me. I’ve been kidnapped.” One day, a pockmarked man in a black Studebaker hears her. He talks about Harry, stitches, and a busted nose. At the next lights, he warns Milly not to talk and shows her a revolver. Milly becomes frightened, but the Studebaker disappears before they reach Richmond. At the Queens Hotel, Forbes goes to speak with the manager while Milly waits in the bar. During lunch, she tells Forbes about the strange man. Forbes thinks she imagined it and says she needs a creative hobby. Milly feels close to him. Later, while Forbes is away, the pockmarked man grabs Milly and drives away in Forbes’s car. She tries to get help from another driver by saying, “Please help me. I’ve been kidnapped.” The driver turns away toward Hampton Court.

Rain carried him into a gutter. Two boys put him in a paper boat. The boat went through a dark tunnel. A water rat demanded his passport, but he stayed silent and brave. The boat sank in a canal, and a fish swallowed him. Later, a cook cut open the fish and found the soldier. He was back in the same room with the dancer. A boy threw him into the stove. The dancer flew into the fire too. The soldier melted into a little tin heart, and only the dancer's black sequin remained.

video_title: 👑 I Want to Go Home! | A Little Princess Story | Read Aloud for Kids

summaries.summary: One day, the Queen found a new castle. She said the old castle was too small because the little princess now had a brother and there were many other people too. The Duke of Somewhere-or-Other bought the old castle, so the little princess moved to the new one. She did not like leaving and kept saying, “I want to go home.” The Queen showed her the big new room, the yard, and the kitchen, but the little princess still wanted to return. At last, the Queen let her visit the old castle for a peep. The Duke lived there now and had painted it. The Duchess showed them the new kitchen and the yard, where the trees were gone. She planned to have tea and cake on the lawn, but she did not want crumbs or birds and had to vacuum the grass every day. The little princess and the Queen both wanted to go home. “There’s no place like home,” said the little princess.

video_title: 📘 Kids Book Read Aloud: BEING FRANK by Donna W. Earnhardt and Andrea Castellani

summaries.summary: Frank always told the truth. He told Dottie her freckles looked like the Big Dipper, told Carol her singing sounded shaky, and told Miss Aroma that her breath smelled funny. He also told Principal Wiggins that his toupee looked like a weasel and told his mother she had wrinkles and was speeding. The children and adults became upset, and Frank felt unhappy. He visited his grandfather, Grandpa Ernest. Grandpa showed Frank how to tell the truth kindly. He praised the good part of Mrs. Peacock’s flower-covered hat and gave Mr. Pickles helpful advice about his relish when Mr. Pickles asked for it. At the school carnival, Frank gave kind comments to Miss Aroma, Mr. Wiggins, Dottie, and Carol. Carol smiled, and Frank rode the Ferris wheel with Dottie. He also gave his mother a kind poem. Later, Frank answered Mrs. Peacock kindly about her unusual hat. Frank learned that honesty is best served with more sugar and less pepper, so it does not hurt people’s feelings.

video_title: 📚 Kids Book Read Aloud: THERE'S A REASON YOU ARE HERE by Sarah and Alex Shortcake

summaries.summary: The speaker tells a child that everything in the world has a reason for being there. Leaves, waves, snow, the universe, and every strand of hair exist for reasons people may not yet understand. The creatures in the deep blue sea also have a purpose, even though they look different from humans. The speaker compares the child to the moon, shooting stars, and crashing thunder, explaining that there is a reason the child is exactly the way they are and does the things they do. The speaker then reveals that, long ago, they prayed every night for the child, so the child is the answer to every prayer. Every freckle, finger, and hair matters to the speaker. The child is also the reason the speaker is here. Although one reason would be enough, the speaker says there are infinite reasons for the child’s existence and ends by expressing happiness that everyone shares the planet.

summaries.summary: Miss Pimento announces that the school will have vision screening day. Carla hopes she will need glasses, so she can be different. During the week, she makes and wears pretend glasses from pipe cleaners, craft sticks, paper, and glitter. At the screening, Carla reads the eye chart well and learns that she does not need glasses. Buster learns that he does need them. At Dr. Olie’s Eyewear, Buster chooses frames, but he feels worried because he likes to blend in and thinks everyone will look at him. Carla wants to help. At home, she cuts, glues, bends, shapes, and paints many pretend glasses. The next morning, she gives them to Miss Pimento. Each child takes a pair. When Buster enters the classroom, he sees that everyone is wearing Carla’s glasses. He laughs and feels better. Carla’s idea helps Buster blend in, and she shows that she is a good friend.

summaries.summary: Aquaman is fair. He plays by the rules, does not cheat, and shares with others, so people can trust him. When he is on the team of the seven seas, he uses his skills to help the team. When he shares a snack with his friends, he divides it evenly so everyone gets the same amount. When Aquaman has trouble, he asks for advice and listens to other people’s ideas because he knows every opinion is important. When he catches evil-doers, he makes sure they receive a punishment that fits what they did. If Aquaman causes an accident, he admits it was his fault and does not blame anyone else. When someone calls for help, Aquaman brings backup and does not leave anyone out. When supervillains attack, he rushes into battle like the rising tide and defeats them fair and square. Aquaman’s actions show that he treats others equally and follows the rules.

video_title: Worry Shy: Story to Help Children Better Understand and Manage Social Anxiety. Read Aloud Kids Book

summaries.summary: Little C felt worried every day about being with other people. He wondered who would be there, what he should say, and whether people would laugh, stare, or think he looked silly. His heart raced, his mouth felt dry, and he wanted to go home. After social events, he kept thinking about everything he had said and wondered if he had done something wrong. One day, Little C told his mother about his worries. She took him to the doctor, who explained that he had social anxiety. The doctor said his body was giving a false alarm, causing fear, a racing heart, and sweaty hands. With help from his doctor and parents, Little C learned coping strategies. He took deep breaths, used positive self-talk, imagined success, challenged negative thoughts, and practiced small social steps with trusted people. He celebrated each win. With time, Little C became more confident. He still felt scared sometimes, but he faced his fears and showed his true self.

video_title: Creepy But Cool Bats | Kids & Family Picture Story Book Time | Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly. They have fur, feed their babies milk, and use thin skin wings stretched between their fingers. Most bats drop from a high place before flying. They are awake at night and sleep during the day. Many eat insects, while others eat fruit, frogs, or fish. The Flying Fox is the largest bat and eats only fruit. Bats help people by spreading seeds and pollen and eating insects that harm crops. They use echolocation: clicks and squeaks bounce off objects and make sound pictures in their brains. Most bats live in dark caves, empty buildings, or trees. Groups are called colonies, and bats often sleep upside down. Mothers usually have one hairless, blind pup each year. The pup clings to its mother and learns to fly and hunt after four to six weeks. People and white nose fungus have harmed bats, so scientists study them and work to help them survive.

The following equations are seven plus seven equals 14, seven plus eight equals 15, and eight plus eight equals 16. Finally, eight plus nine makes 17, nine plus nine makes 18, nine plus 10 makes 19, and 10 plus 10 makes 20 garbage trucks. Each equation increases the total as the two groups of garbage trucks become larger.

summaries.summary: Splat the Cat became the new student body president because he was the only student who ran. Everyone cheered, almost. Her mother came from India, and her father came from Jamaica. Her first name honors her Indian background. As a child, Harris attended civil rights protests with her parents, which motivated her to pursue a career in law. She later spoke at events marking the 50th anniversary of the signing of the Civil Rights Act. Harris graduated from Howard University with a degree in political science and attended law school at the University of California at Hastings in 2003. She became San Francisco’s district attorney and was elected California’s attorney general in 2010. Harris began a presidential campaign in January 2019 but ended it nearly a year later because she lacked enough money to continue. Joe Biden won the Democratic nomination and chose Harris as his running mate. They won the November 2020 election, and Harris became vice president on January 20, 2021.

After dinner, Nancy made a trophy for Jack.
