video_title: Seeing Symmetry (symmetry in nature, art, & everyday objects, helping kids recognize) #kids #story

summaries.summary: Symmetry means that parts match like mirror images. A sea turtle has a line of symmetry from its nose to its tail, with one flipper matching the other, although nature is not always exact. Many animals, including scallops, beetles, lizards, penguins, and whales, have this kind of symmetry. A person’s body, face, hands together, and some clothes also show matching sides. Some letters and words, such as A, O, mom, and aha, have lines of symmetry. Some symmetry happens when a shape spins around a center point. This is called rotational symmetry. A Z can look the same after turning halfway around. Flowers, pinwheels, stars, snowflakes, kaleidoscope shapes, and some life forms show rotational symmetry. Animals use matching legs, fins, or wings to move. Machines such as helicopters, gears, bicycles, and wind turbines have spinning symmetrical parts. People use symmetry in art, decorations, buildings, furniture, and most vehicles. Symmetry can be found almost anywhere.

Flowers, pinwheels, stars, snowflakes, kaleidoscope shapes, and quilt blocks can have rotational symmetry. Animals use matching legs, fins, or wings to crawl, swim, hop, walk, run, or fly. Machines such as helicopters, gears, wind turbines, bicycles, and waterwheels use symmetrical rotating parts. People have used symmetry in art, decorations, holiday symbols, buildings, furniture, and vehicles for a long time. The text encourages readers to look for symmetry almost anywhere.

video_title: Zachary Zormer: Shape Transformer (about thinking critically & solving problems) #kids #learn #story

summaries.summary: On Friday, Zachary Zor forgets to bring something fun to measure. Tyler shows an Orchid flower that is 8 inches wide. Zach uses a paper strip to make a Mobius strip. Though the strip is 8 1/2 inches long, the loop measures 17 inches, and the class makes its own loops. The next Friday, Zach loses his picture frame. Tyler shows a 400-million-year-old fossil with a 6-inch perimeter. Zach cuts a 4-by-6-inch Hall Pass into a zigzag frame large enough to walk through. The paper stays the same size, but its edges become much longer. On another Friday, Zach leaves his backpack in the car. Tyler shows a small war medal with an area of 1 square inch. Zach uses a tiny flashlight and angles its beam to cover 40 square inches. He explains that slanted sunlight spreads out and helps cause winter. Zach tells Tyler he invents ideas as he goes. Tyler likes the flashlight idea, and they plan to build a Mobius space track together.

It becomes part of everything, and the narrator understands that an idea can change the world.

summaries.summary: Tony was a curious little aunt who often explored far from his anthill. One day, he found Bella, a sheep sitting sadly away from her flock in a meadow. Bella wanted to see the world, but she was afraid to go alone. Tony offered to guide her, so he climbed onto her wool and they began their journey. They crossed a bubbling brook using a sturdy log and entered the forest. Tony showed Bella tall trees, bright wild flowers, sweet clover, and tiny mushrooms. Bella became braver because Tony stayed beside her. Then a hungry fox came from the bushes. Tony found a narrow path that was too small for the fox but large enough for Bella. Bella followed him, and the fox gave up. When they returned, Bella told the other sheep about their adventure. She was no longer timid, and the sheep began exploring too. Tony and Bella showed that courage and friendship help face challenges.

On Ian’s sixteenth birthday, Laurel gave him a wizard’s staff, a phoenix gem, and a spell from their dead father. The spell could bring Dad back for one day. Barley tried the magic, but Ian made their father appear. The gem broke before the spell was finished, so only Dad’s legs came back. The brothers had to find another phoenix gem before sunset the next day. They traveled in Barley’s van, Guinevere, to the Manticore’s Tavern. The Manticore gave them a children’s menu instead of a map, then destroyed the tavern when Ian said she was no longer daring. Ian saved Dad’s legs from a falling beam. Following the menu to Ravens Point, the brothers met Pixie Dusters. Ian drove Guinevere with Barley’s help, and they escaped the sprites.

summaries.summary: Doug, a golden retriever, hikes with his friends Carl Frederickson and Russell to find a camping place. His talking collar makes him say, “Find the spot!” Doug finds a clearing with trees and a view. They set up tents, cook dinner, and roast marshmallows. Russell sees paw prints near the campfire. Doug promises to stay awake and guard the camp while Carl and Russell sleep. During the night, Doug chases a squirrel and accidentally breaks part of Russell’s tent. Then a bat surprises him, and he spills the lemonade. Later, Doug sees a raccoon trying to take sausages from the picnic basket. He pulls the sausages away from the raccoon and saves the breakfast. Near morning, Doug becomes very tired and falls asleep. Carl wakes up and sees the messy sausages and spilled lemonade. Doug tells Carl about the creature. Carl pats him and says, “Good dog.” Then Doug and Carl watch the sun rise.

summaries.summary: One morning on the farm, Rowley saw Nanny pick apples. He knew she would bake an apple pie. Rowley ran inside to tell his siblings, but Patch and Penny were watching Thunderbolt and pretending to be fire heroes. They raced around the house, spilling milk and eggs. Pongo and Perdita took the puppies to the barn for fire safety training. Patch and Penny coiled their hoses and climbed a ladder quickly. Rowley tangled his hose and fell from the ladder because he was afraid of heights. Then the puppies raced to the fire hydrant. Rowley fell behind, but he smelled smoke. He ran to the kitchen and barked loudly. Nanny had forgotten the pie in the oven, and it was burning. Roger and Anita opened the door and window while Nanny turned off the oven. Everyone called Rowley a hero. At the firehouse, Rowley met firefighters and received a fire helmet. The puppies learned that being brave and helpful mattered more than being the fastest or strongest.

video_title: Disney/Pixar Elemental: A Family's Dream | A Read-Along Storybook in HD

summaries.summary: Bernie and Cinder Lumen move to Element City to follow their dreams. Their daughter, Ember, grows up helping in their fire shop. Bernie wants Ember to take over, but she must learn to control her anger. During a busy sale, Ember gets angry and breaks a pipe. Water floods the shop, and Inspector Wade arrives with tickets that may close it. Ember and Wade learn that a broken canal gate caused the flood. Ember uses her hot fire to turn sandbags into a strong glass wall, stopping the leak. Wade sees her glass-making talent, and they begin to care about each other. Bernie later gives Ember the new shop sign, but Ember does not want the shop; it is Bernie’s dream, not hers. She sends Wade away because she fears hurting her family. When the glass wall breaks, Wade returns to help. He disappears as steam after Ember tells him she loves him. Ember tells Bernie the truth, and he says he wants her to be happy. Wade returns, and Ember follows her heart.

video_title: The Christmas Day Kitten by James Herriot - Children's Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Mr. Harriet first sees Debbie, a shy tabby cat, at Mrs. Pickering’s house. Debbie is a stray who comes for food, sits by the warm fire with the three basset hounds, and then quietly leaves. She will not stay or let people help her. One Christmas morning, Debbie returns carrying a tiny kitten. She is very thin and sick, so Mrs. Pickering cares for her. Debbie dies, and Mrs. Pickering keeps the kitten. She names him Buster. Buster grows into a healthy, happy cat who lives with Mrs. Pickering and the basset hounds. A year later, on Christmas Day, Buster plays with the dogs and fetches a ball from the garden again and again. Mrs. Pickering holds him and remembers Debbie bringing him to her home. She says Debbie would be pleased. Mrs. Pickering calls Buster the best Christmas present she has ever had.

video_title: Building by Henry Cole - Children's Book Read Aloud

summaries.summary: In late winter, two beavers find a good place for a home beside a small stream, near willow and maple trees. They use their strong teeth and jaws to chew down trees and cut the branches into pieces. They carry the branches to the stream and stick them in the mud. Soon they build a dam, which holds back water and makes a pond. In the pond, they build a dome-shaped lodge with an underwater passageway. The mother beaver has babies there, and she nurses them until they grow strong. When the babies explore, their parents slap their tails to warn them about a coyote. The young beavers dive safely into the lodge. They grow bigger and eat twigs and bark. A thunderstorm damages the dam, so the family rebuilds it. Ducks, blackbirds, butterflies, swallows, dragonflies, and turtles live in the pond. Before winter, the beavers gather food and stay warm under snow and ice.

summaries.summary: Mickey Mouse decorated his living room with ghosts, spiders, bats, and a jack-o'-lantern for his Halloween party. While making popcorn balls, he saw moving shadows outside, but they were only branches and leaves. He went to the attic to find his pirate costume. A coat rack covered with a sheet looked like a ghost, and a skeleton popped out of an old trunk. Mickey learned they were only decorations and carried the trunk downstairs. Outside, Pluto got covered by a sheet while chasing a ball. Rain made the sheet stick to him, so he could not see. Donald, Goofy, Minnie, and Daisy arrived during a storm. The lights went out, and they heard the trunk and Mickey moving upstairs. They thought the house was haunted. Mickey came downstairs in his pirate costume, carrying the skeleton, and scared them. When the lights came on, they saw Mickey. Then Pluto ran inside under the wet sheet and scared everyone again. Mickey dried Pluto, and they called it the scariest Halloween ever.

video_title: MICKEY MOUSE in THE SORCERER'S APPRENTICE | Bedtime Story for Kids

summaries.summary: A great sorcerer knew all about magic. His Magic Hat made magic happen when he thought of something. His helper, Mickey, did all the work, such as sweeping, chopping wood, and carrying water. One day, the sorcerer went out. Mickey put on the Magic Hat and made an old broom come alive. The broom grew arms and feet and carried buckets of water. Mickey sat down and fell asleep because he thought he would never work again. The broom kept working and flooded the room. Mickey tried to stop it, but he could not. He chopped the broom with an ax, but every piece became a new broom. Soon, many brooms brought more water, and Mickey was nearly covered. He found the sorcerer’s magic book, but the swirling water stopped him from reading it. Then the sorcerer returned and used magic to stop the brooms and water. He told Mickey, “Don’t start what you can’t finish.” Mickey went back to work.

video_title: A Mystery In Paris

summaries.summary: Mickey, Minnie, and Goofy visit Paris in spring. Goofy mistakes the Arc de Triomphe for a bridge and the Eiffel Tower for an oil well. Mickey loses his wallet, so he and Minnie return to a restaurant. While they are gone, a disguised man tells Goofy that he owns the Eiffel Tower. Goofy pays him all his money, 222 cents, to buy it. Mickey explains that the tower belongs to Paris, so they report the trick to Inspector Pierre. Pierre says this has happened four times that month. Mickey disguises Goofy, and the same man tries to sell the tower again. They follow him to his home, where they discover his hungry children. The man is a poor actor who used costumes to trick people. Inspector Pierre agrees that he can work at a souvenir store and repay the people he cheated. The next morning, Goofy buys a small Notre Dame souvenir, not the real cathedral.

video_title: Nate the Great and the Earth Day Robot

summaries.summary: Nate the Great is a student and detective. His class has made Mr. Butler, a little solar robot that says, “Yum yum dirt!” and cleans floors. But Mr. Butler disappears before the Earth Day Fair. Nate searches the school. A video shows Dusty the custodian whistling at night, which starts Mr. Butler. A robot cat, Hightech Hex, chases Mr. Butler into room 238. Nate searches there, then rooms with fake soil and giant earthworms, but finds nothing. At home, Nate tells Sludge, his dog. Sludge digs a hole and makes a mound. Nate understands that Sludge has found a clue. The next day, Nate digs in the mound and finds Mr. Butler. The robot is weak because its batteries are empty and it is full of dirt. Nate cleans and charges it. At the fair, Mr. Butler cleans dirt and wins praise. Then he vacuums up the fake soil, while Hightech Hex guards against the dark cloud. Sludge has solved the mystery.

video_title: Henry and Mudge and the Great Grandpas

summaries.summary: On a sunny summer day, Henry, his dog Mudge, and Henry’s parents visited Great Grandpa Bill. Great Grandpa Bill lived with many other grandpas. Henry brought them books, magazines, candies, puzzles, and cards. The grandpas liked Henry and Mudge, and they petted Mudge and rested on him. While the parents visited, Henry and Mudge explored the woods. They found a pretty clearing with flowers, birds, butterflies, and a swimming pond. Henry wanted to swim, but he knew he could not swim alone. He told his parents, and Dad, Great Grandpa Bill, and all the grandpas wanted to swim too. They walked to the pond, resting on Mudge along the way. Everyone swam in their underwear. Mudge carried tired grandpas like a raft. After swimming and hearing stories, they returned home. Henry’s mother made spaghetti, and everyone ate. At sunset, they rested in rocking chairs, happy to be together at the grandpa house.

video_title: a kids book about death... (to be read with an adult)

summaries.summary: This book explains death and the big feelings it can bring. A living person’s body works, thinks, and feels. Dying begins when important body parts, called vital organs, stop working. These include the lungs, heart, kidneys, liver, and brain. Being sick or hurt does not always mean dying. People may die because they are very old, badly hurt, or have a serious illness. Dying can happen quickly or slowly. A dying person may become tired or eat less, and others help them feel calm and comfortable. Death is when the whole body stops working. Families may honor a dead person with a funeral, songs, prayers, burial, cremation, or other choices. Death is normal, and it is okay to talk about it. People can remember someone who died by telling stories, saying their name, visiting a special place, writing a letter, or listening to a favorite song. Love and grief can continue after death.

Dying begins when vital organs, such as the heart, lungs, brain, kidneys, or liver, stop working. Sickness or an injury is not always dying, but old age, serious illness, or a major accident can cause death. When someone dies, the body stops working completely. Families show respect in different ways, such as having a funeral, burial, cremation, prayers, songs, or a memorial. Death is a normal part of life, and talking about it can help people remember and celebrate someone who died. Love does not end with death. Grief is what people feel as they carry that love. They can remember someone by telling stories, visiting special places, writing letters, or sharing favorite foods and songs.

video_title: Sir Cumference and the Sword in the Cone

summaries.summary: One morning at King Arthur’s castle, Vertex told his friend Radius that five knights were trying to become the next king. They had to find the hidden sword, Edgecaliber, by solving a puzzle. With help from Circumference, Lady Dye, and the carpenters Geo and Sim, Vertex and Radius folded the parchment pictures into solid shapes. They counted each shape’s faces, points, and edges. Adding the faces and points, then subtracting the edges, gave two for every shape except the cylinder and cone. The clue said, “Three times as tall as its base is wide.” The friends searched the castle’s round towers and then dug up cones under the courtyard. After measuring many cones, Vertex found one that fit the clue. Edgecaliber was hidden inside it. King Arthur praised Vertex’s clever work and named him the future king. Vertex later became a wise king. The counting rule is called Euler’s law.

video_title: Magic In The Mist

summaries.summary: Thomas lived in a small, leaky hut beside a bog in West Wales. He was learning to be a wizard, but his spells were too weak to light the fire or keep the rain and wind out. His only friend was Jeremy, a little toad who could listen to the wind and hum its song. One day, Jeremy hummed a new tune, and the wind suddenly became quiet. Thomas went outside and found a tiny green dragon trembling in the marsh grass. He carried the dragon into the hut, gave it fish and water, and cared for it with Jeremy. Later, Thomas tried to light the fire, but his magic failed again. The dragon breathed a small flame onto the wood and started the fire. Jeremy sang a song that sounded like the fire, and Thomas asked to learn it. That night, the dragon left. Thomas and Jeremy stayed in the warm, cheerful hut, where their shared music helped Thomas’s magic work better.

video_title: Henry and Mudge and the Tumbling Trip

summaries.summary: One day, Henry learns that he, Mudge, and his parents are going on vacation to the Wild West. Henry is excited about cowboy boots and hats. His father jokes that Mudge can round up cows, though Mudge would probably kiss them. The family drives west. The land becomes flatter, the skies bigger, and the people taller. At the Cowboy Inn, Henry gets a cowboy hat and Mudge gets a bandana. Henry and Mudge chase tumbleweeds until dark and collect 42 of them. When the vacation ends, they drive home. Henry and Mudge enjoy being home again, where many fun things are waiting under Henry’s bed. They loved the Wild West, but they loved home best.

video_title: Norma Jean, Jumping Bean

summaries.summary: Norma Jean loved to jump. She jumped out of bed, into her clothes, down the stairs, and all the way to school. At school, she could not sit still for Miss Jones’s story. She jumped while playing with Nell and knocked down their block tower. At lunch, she jumped and spilled milk on Sam. After school, she bounced too hard on Ted’s seesaw, and he stopped playing. Then she jumped into Amy’s pool, so Amy went inside. Norma Jean understood why her friends were upset. The next day, she stopped jumping, even when she saw a puddle, friends jumping rope, and school jumping contests. At field day, Ted won the egg and spoon race, Amy and Sam won the wheelbarrow race, and Nell won the rope climbing contest. Norma Jean then entered the hurdles, high jump, and potato sack race and won them all. Miss Jones gave her a blue ribbon naming her champion jumping bean. Norma Jean jumped for joy all the way home.

video_title: Smile a Lot!

summaries.summary: The story says that life has ups and downs, so you should always “Smile a lot.” When Mom makes oatmeal with prunes, smiling is better than complaining. You can ask to help make chocolate chip pancakes another day and decide what to do with the oatmeal. If you are the new kid at school, smiling can help you make friends. If tough kids take the swings, you can play on the monkey bars and smile until they leave the swings. If you get only three words right on a spelling test, smile, tell Mom and Dad you will do better, and study hard for next time. A smile can also give you courage at the dentist, where you might get a prize for being brave. At soccer practice, smiling uses less energy than moaning, so you may run fast and play forward. At bedtime, smile because you had a pretty good day.

video_title: Under Our Clothes - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook

summaries.summary: People have bodies of many shapes and sizes, and every body deserves care and respect. People may choose different amounts of clothing and privacy because of their families, cultures, and feelings. Privacy means having personal space and choosing who may see or touch your body. Private parts are covered by underwear or bathing suits. A doctor or trusted caregiver may help keep a child clean or healthy, but touching must be safe. Children can say no to hugs, kisses, or any touch they do not want. This is called consent. They should tell a trusted adult about unsafe touching or secrets. Bodies and feelings change as children grow, especially during puberty. Some people feel worried about how they look. Pictures in media may be changed, and body shaming can hurt people. Everyone looks and feels different. Children can build self-esteem by accepting themselves, using kind self-talk, caring for their feelings, and noticing the good qualities in themselves and their friends.

She teaches Rosie by using her eyes to measure, her hands to feel, and her mouth to taste. As Abuela makes each tamale, she shares wishes: flexibility from the softened corn husk, protection from its covering, pride from the masa, food and spice from the filling, love from an olive, hugs from the folds, and family support from the tamales resting together. Rosie and the family make dozens of tamales and wait for them to steam. After several hours, they unwrap and eat them. Abuela sings, “Deliciosa! video_title: Jackie Robinson - He Led the Way - Kids Read Aloud Audiobook

summaries.summary: Jackie Robinson was born in Georgia in 1919. When he was young, his family moved to Pasadena, California. Jackie faced unfair treatment because he was Black, but his mother told him to stand up for himself. Jackie loved sports and became a star in football, baseball, basketball, and the long jump. After World War II, he played for the Kansas City Monarchs. Branch Rickey, president of the Brooklyn Dodgers, asked Jackie to join the Dodgers and promised that Jackie would face cruel words and unfair treatment. Jackie agreed not to fight back. In 1947, he became the first Black player in the major leagues. Some people insulted him, but Jackie played wonderfully and helped the Dodgers. He was Rookie of the Year and later the National League’s Most Valuable Player. In 1955, the Dodgers won the World Series. Jackie later worked for equal rights and became the first Black player in the Baseball Hall of Fame. He showed that talent is not based on skin color.

At night, a viper fish blinks a light to attract small fish and eats them with sharp fangs. A green bomber worm releases green glowing balls to distract a predator and escape. Deep-ocean creatures use light to find food, seek mates, and protect themselves.

video_title: The Lion and the Mouse | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: In Africa, a strong and fierce lion lived near a great tree. All the animals were afraid of him. One day, a little mouse ran across the sleeping lion’s nose. The lion caught her and said he would eat her. The mouse asked him to let her go and promised to help him someday. The lion laughed because she was so small, but he felt kind and released her. Days later, the lion stepped into a hunter’s net. He pulled and roared, but the ropes wrapped around him tighter. The little mouse heard him and found him trapped. She remembered her promise. The mouse crawled into the net and chewed through the ropes. The lion became free and felt embarrassed. He had learned that a small creature could help a great creature. You are never too big or too small to give or receive kindness.

video_title: The Lion and the Mouse | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: In the African grassland, a powerful lion frightened every animal. He rested beneath a great tree while a small mouse, fleeing from an eagle, accidentally ran across his nose. The lion caught her and threatened to eat her. The mouse begged for her life and promised that she would repay his kindness someday. The lion laughed because she was tiny, but he suddenly decided to release her, so she hurried away. Days later, the lion became trapped in a hunter’s net after failing to notice it hidden behind a bush. He struggled, roared, and cried, but only became more tangled. Nearby, the mouse heard him and discovered that the trapped animal was the lion who had spared her. Although she could have left, she remembered her promise. She crawled through the net and chewed through the ropes until the lion was free. The embarrassed lion learned that even a small creature can help someone powerful. The story shows that no one is too big or too small to give or receive kindness.

video_title: Country Mouse and City Mouse | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: Country Mouse lived in a small burrow in the country, where he enjoyed birds, bees, flowers, and stars. His friend, City Mouse, lived downtown and liked cars, sidewalks, and bright city lights. Country Mouse invited City Mouse to visit. City Mouse disliked the dirty fields, cow smells, dark burrow, and simple meal of dried corn and peas. He returned to the city and invited Country Mouse to visit him. A few days later, Country Mouse went to the city. City Mouse showed him a large home and a table filled with sausage, cheese, grapes, cake, and cookies. The mice began to eat, but an angry cat chased them into a wall hole. When they returned, a cook saw them and tried to kill them, so they ran away again. Country Mouse decided the rich food was not worth being frightened. He returned to his peaceful country burrow, while City Mouse stayed in the city.

video_title: Country Mouse and City Mouse | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: Country Mouse lived peacefully in a luxurious burrow in the country, enjoying birds, bees, flowers, and stars. His friend, City Mouse, lived downtown and preferred cars, footsteps, and bright city lights. Country Mouse invited City Mouse to visit, but City Mouse disliked the dirt, smells, dark burrow, and simple meal of dried corn and peas. He returned to the city and invited Country Mouse to visit him. In the city, Country Mouse saw City Mouse’s large home and a table filled with sausage, cheese, crackers, grapes, cake, and cookies. While they feasted, an angry cat appeared, forcing them to hide in a wall. When they returned to eat, a cook discovered them and chased them away again. City Mouse accepted these dangers as part of his luxurious life, but Country Mouse decided the food was not worth being constantly frightened. He returned to his quiet burrow, and the two friends continued living happily, one in the country and one in the city.

video_title: The Ugly Duckling | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: Near a pond, a mother duck sits on her eggs and keeps them warm. Frogs croak, fish splash, and insects buzz while she waits. Soon the eggs hatch, and several ducklings join her. The last egg hatches later. Its baby is bigger and looks different, so the mother duck pushes him away. The other ducklings peck him and will not play with him. The sad duckling tries to find friends. A kitten is busy chasing a mouse, and an old dog wants to sleep. No one plays with him. The duckling finds other ways to be happy. He chases bugs, eats seeds, plays in water, jumps in puddles, and explores new places. As he grows, he meets large birds at another pond. He sees that he looks like them. He is not a duckling. He is a swan. The other swans let him eat, play, and float with them. He feels happy because he belongs with the swans.

video_title: The Ugly Duckling | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: At a pond, a mother duck waits patiently on her eggs while frogs croak, fish splash, and insects buzz. One by one, her ducklings hatch, but the last baby looks different, is larger, and is not pretty to her. The mother duck pushes him away, and the other ducklings peck at him and refuse to play. The sad duckling stays near them while learning, eating, and growing, then leaves to search for friends. A kitten is too busy chasing a mouse, and an old dog only wants to sleep and eat. Alone, the duckling finds bugs, seeds, puddles, and new places to explore. As he grows, he meets a group of large birds with long necks. He discovers that he is not a duck but a swan. His feathers become beautiful, and the other swans welcome him. They float, eat, and play together while watching the sunset. The swan is happy to belong with them.

video_title: Daniel and His Friends | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: Daniel and his friends were taken from their homes by an invading army. They were taught to become advisors to the king. The boys were given unhealthy food, but Daniel and his friends bravely asked for good food. God helped them grow strong and healthy, and the king saw that they were wise. Later, the king had a dream that no one could explain. He became angry and planned to kill his advisors. Daniel and his friends prayed, and God showed Daniel the dream and its meaning, so they were saved. When the king told people to worship an idol, Daniel’s friends refused. They were thrown into a fire, but God kept them safe. Later, King Darius ruled. Jealous advisers made a law that people must pray to the king. Daniel kept praying to God, so he was thrown into a den of hungry lions. Daniel prayed, and God sent angels to close the lions’ mouths. Daniel was safe because he followed God.

video_title: Daniel and His Friends | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: When Daniel and his friends were boys, an invading army took them from their homes to train as advisors to the king. They asked to eat wholesome food instead of the unhealthy food provided. God helped them become strong and wise, and the king was impressed. Later, the king had a troubling dream that no advisor could explain. Daniel and his friends prayed, and God revealed the dream and its meaning to Daniel, saving their lives. When the king ordered everyone to worship an idol, Daniel’s friends refused because of their faith. They were thrown into a fire, but God kept them safe. Daniel continued obeying God after King Darius became ruler. Jealous advisers tricked Darius into making a law against praying to God. Daniel kept praying, so he was thrown into a den of hungry lions. Daniel prayed, and God sent angels to shut the lions’ mouths. The next morning, Darius found Daniel alive and praised God for protecting him.

video_title: David & Goliath | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: David was a young shepherd boy in Israel. He played the harp for King Saul and cared for his father’s sheep while his three older brothers fought the Philistines. One day, David brought food to his brothers and the army. He saw Goliath of Gath, a huge soldier who challenged the Israelites to fight him. David said he would fight Goliath. King Saul worried because David was only a boy, but David said God had helped him save sheep from a lion and a bear. Saul gave David armor, but it was too heavy, so David took it off. He picked up five smooth stones and carried his sling. Goliath laughed at David, but David said he came in the name of the Lord. David used his sling to throw one stone. It hit Goliath’s forehead, and Goliath fell dead. David cut off Goliath’s head, and the Philistines ran away.

video_title: David & Goliath | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: David was a young shepherd in Israel who played the harp for King Saul. While David cared for his sheep, his three older brothers fought the Philistines. One day, David carried corn to his brothers and cheese to King Saul’s army. He saw Goliath of Gath, a gigantic, heavily armored warrior, challenge the Israelites to send one man to fight him. David offered to fight because God had helped him defeat a lion and a bear. King Saul gave David armor, but it was too heavy, so David removed it. He took his sling and gathered five smooth stones from a brook. Goliath mocked him, but David said he came in the name of the Lord. When Goliath charged, David ran toward him and struck his forehead with one stone from his sling. Goliath fell and died. David used Goliath’s sword to cut off his head, and the frightened Philistines ran away. David saved his people from slavery.

video_title: The Princess and the Pea | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: Long ago, a prince wanted to marry a true princess. One stormy night, a woman came to the castle. She was soaked, and she said her name was Princess Anne. The queen wanted to test her. She told servants to place a small, dried pea under 20 feather beds. The queen thought a true princess would feel the pea and sleep badly. In the morning, Anne said she had not slept well. The queen was happy, but a servant told her that they had forgotten to put the pea under the beds. The prince asked Anne why she had slept badly. Anne said she had been thinking about the townspeople, their crops, and their animals during the storm. The prince saw that Anne was kind and good. He and Anne helped people in town, chased chickens, mended fences, and served food. Soon they married, and the kingdom celebrated. Everyone learned that caring for others is truly important.

video_title: The Princess and the Pea | Narrated Stories | The Good and the Beautiful

summaries.summary: Long ago, a prince had everything he wanted except a wife. He told the king and queen that he would marry only a true princess, so they began searching. During a terrible storm, a soaked stranger arrived at the castle and said she was Princess Anne. The queen wanted to test her, so she placed twenty feather beds over a dried pea. In the morning, Anne said she had slept poorly. The queen rejoiced, but a servant admitted that they had forgotten to put the pea under the beds. The prince asked Anne why she had not slept well. Anne explained that she had been worried about the townsfolk, their crops, and their animals during the storm. The prince recognized her kind heart. He and Anne then helped the townspeople repair fences, find chickens, and serve food. They married soon afterward, and the kingdom learned that caring for others showed what was truly important.

video_title: Field Trip Fiasco 🐘🦒🦜 by Julie Danneberg

summaries.summary: Mrs. Hartwell’s class is excited for a field trip to the zoo. She prepares a list of tips and a just-in-case bag. Before leaving, she gives everyone animal observation sheets and jobs. On the bus, she discovers Eddie is still in the bathroom, so she takes attendance. When the bus breaks down, she shares animal crackers. At the zoo, the students count 26 people instead of 24, but Jack and Alexandra find two boys from another class. At the petting zoo, Alexandra trips over a hay bale, and Madison trips over her. An elephant sprays Eddie, and he needs dry clothes. In the aviary, a bird drops something wet and white on Eddie’s head. The zookeeper calls it good luck and gives Eddie a badge and a free pass. Mrs. Hartwell lets the class stop writing and enjoy observing. They watch animals, then finish their sheets at school and share what they learned. She learns that field trips need focus, learning, and fun.

video_title: Carrot Delight 🎪🐇 by Brian Mangas 📚 Kids Book #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Father Rabbit told Honey Bunny he was going to the hardware store and would not stop for ice cream or the park. Honey promised Mother Rabbit that she would not fuss. On the drive to town, Honey and Father Rabbit counted trucks, station wagons, and a police car. At the hardware store, Honey behaved very well. Father Rabbit then offered her ice cream, but Honey remembered her promise and said no, even when he told her they had carrot delight. On the way home, traffic stopped because a circus was in the street. Father Rabbit saw elephants and clowns and wanted to stop, but Honey said they should go home. They rode home quietly. Mother Rabbit asked if Honey had kept her promise, and Honey said yes. Mother Rabbit decided to take Honey for ice cream and to the circus. Father Rabbit said he wanted to go too. He said he would tell them why on the way.

video_title: The Good Little Bad Little Pig 🐖 by Margaret Wise Brown 📚 Kids Book #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Peter asked his mother for a pig. He wanted a clean pig that was both good and bad. Peter and his mother wrote to a farmer. The farmer had five little pigs. Three were good, one was bad, and one was a good little bad little pig, so he sent that pig to Peter. The pig was dirty and ran around squealing. Peter’s family called him bad, but Peter said they should wait and get to know him. The pig followed Peter and ate bread and milk, though he made a mess. Peter gave him a warm bath and scrubbed him until he was clean. Then Peter took him for a walk. A policeman stopped the cars so they could cross. The pig first refused to move, but then he crossed nicely. The people called him good. Peter got what he wanted: a good little bad little pig who was sometimes good and sometimes bad.

video_title: The Good Little Bad Little Pig 🐖 by Margaret Wise Brown 📚 Kids Book #Read Aloud

video_title: The Good Little Bad Little Pig 🐖 by Margaret Wise Brown 📚 Kids Book #Read Aloud

The pig squealed, jumped from its box, and ran around, so Peter’s family called it bad. Peter said they should wait until it knew them. The pig followed Peter, and Peter’s grandmother called it good, but its noisy eating manners made her change her mind. Peter gave the pig a warm bath and scrubbed it until its white soap turned black and the pig was clean. During a walk, a policeman stopped traffic so Peter and the pig could cross. The pig refused to move, causing cars to honk, but then it crossed nicely. The people called it good. Peter got the good little bad little pig he wanted. Sometimes it was good and sometimes bad, but it was the best pig for Peter.

video_title: 🐶 Muddy Paws Day at the Farm 🐄 by Steve Smallman 📚 Kids Book #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Ben and his puppy, Muddy Paws, were best friends who loved playing together. One morning, Ben learned that he was visiting a farm and could bring Muddy Paws. At the farm, Ben wanted to feed the animals, but Muddy Paws wanted to jump in the muddy puddles. He tried to jump into the duck pond too, so Ben held his leash. In the barn, Ben fed the goats. A greedy goat bumped Ben, and Muddy Paws ran out of the barn and disappeared. Ben searched by the cows, ducks, and muddy pigpen, but he could not find his puppy. A friendly farmer offered Ben a ride on his green tractor to look around the farm. The children helped search. Then they saw something moving under the straw. It was Muddy Paws. Ben hugged him, and Muddy Paws wagged his tail. On the way home, Muddy Paws slept, tired from splashing and playing.

video_title: 🩺 Doctor Pig 🐽🐖 by Emily Gale 📚 Kids Book #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Finley Pig was happy, but Agatha Chicken called him “Lazy bones” because the farm was busy. Finley said he was not lazy and wanted to be a big help. He sat under a tree and thought about what he could do. Then he decided to become Dr Pig. Finley hurried to see his first patients. Mrs. Moo told him that nothing was wrong with her legs and asked him to hold still. Chester Sheep would not stop munching while Finley tried to listen to him. The geese, Heidi and Door, refused to take their medicine. The sheep dog ran away. Being a doctor was hard work, and the chickens were the most difficult patients. At the end of the long day, Mommy Pig was pleased to see Finley. Finley said he was good at being a doctor, but he was even better at being himself. Then he felt happy again.

video_title: 🦆 Duck Stays in the Truck by Doreen Cronin & Betsy Lewis 🛻 Kids Book #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Farmer Brown goes camping with his brother Bob and the animals. He packs a tent and drives toward Breezy Lake. Bob reads the map, but they end up at the library. Bob says they need books for camping, so everyone chooses a book. Then Duck sits in front with the map. Duck points the way, and Farmer Brown drives until they reach a sign that says, “Welcome to Breezy Lake.” Farmer Brown wants everyone to hike, fish, and picnic together. The chickens turn left and hike up the mountain. The pigs turn right and have a picnic in the shade. The cows walk straight ahead to fish. Duck stays in the truck. Farmer Brown and Bob set up the tent. Bob lights a campfire and prepares marshmallows. The chickens, pigs, and cows return when they see the campfire. Then Duck gets out of the truck. Everyone can sit, read, and toast marshmallows together.

video_title: Albert's Field Trip 🍎 by Leslie Tryon 📚 Kids #Story #Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Ryan got measles and could not go on the class trip to Georgie and Gracie’s apple farm. Albert drove the bus and told the children to use good bus manners. They sang about a codling worm. At the farm, Gracie introduced them to Georgie. Each child received a basket and picked red apples from the trees. Then they put the apples in a washer, where they were cleaned and sorted. In the cold storage room, they saw many boxes of apples. Bess put their apples in a juicer, and the children drank the juice. They also ate little apple pies, although Adam dropped his pie. Georgie gave them a baby apple tree, called a sapling, for the schoolyard. The children filled their baskets with different apples and rode home. It was dark when they returned, and their parents took them home and tucked them into bed. The children thanked Georgie and Gracie and said they would watch the tree grow.

video_title: With Love, Little Red Hen 💖 by Alma Flor Ada 📚 #Read Aloud #Stories for Kids

summaries.summary: Little Red Hen moves to Happy Valley with her seven chicks. Mr. Dog, Mr. Goose, and Mr. Cat refuse to help her clear and plant the field, so she does the work herself while her chicks keep her company. Little Red Riding Hood sees the hen and chicks singing as they care for the corn. Goldilocks decides that she, Peter Rabbit and his sisters, and the three pigs should help. Meanwhile, Wolfie and another wolf plan to wait until the corn is ripe and capture the hen. Little Red Hen is later carried away in a sack, but she cuts it open with her scissors, puts in a stone, sews it shut, and runs home. Her corn grows well, and a scarecrow appears in the field. Mr. Cat secretly watches her but falls asleep. Friends help harvest the corn and gather at her house. The wolves hurry to the feast, while the friends enjoy the food and fill the pantry for winter.

video_title: Storytime Channel for Kids: A Piece of the Sky

summaries.summary: The story says that when each person is born, God gives them a special piece of the sky to color and light. It may hold stars, clouds, the sun, or the moon, but it also shines with the person’s heart, dreams, and true self. Whenever a dream comes true or the person simply acts like themselves, their piece of the sky shines brightly. However, being yourself can be difficult when you compare yourself with others or hide the qualities that make you unique. When someone feels afraid, out of place, or hurt by another person’s words, the story offers a reminder to breathe deeply and say, “I can do hard things, I can be brave, I'm the best me God ever made.” Everyone has a piece of the sky, so there is room for every person to be themselves. The story ends by saying that God watches over each person and dreams of them as a precious gift.

video_title: 🤩 Lights! Camera! Alice! 🎥 Kids Book Women's History Month Early Cinema Read Aloud Story

summaries.summary: Alice was a little girl who loved stories. After an earthquake, fire, robbers, and her papa’s death ruined her family’s business, she learned to type and found work at a camera company. There she saw a new camera that made moving pictures. Alice decided to use it to tell stories. She made costumes, sets, and films with actors. She used tricks to make hats dance, people fly, and movies have color and sound. Rival filmmakers tried to steal her ideas, but Alice kept creating. She married a cameraman and moved to America. With her baby, she returned to work and made exciting films, including a pirate ship explosion and a tiger scene. She built the Solax Company studio in Fort Lee, New Jersey. Later, war, illness, and money problems changed the movie business. Hollywood became powerful, audiences left, and Solax was sold. Alice returned to France with her children, still carrying one last story without an ending.

Papa was away at war, and Mama was sick, so nine-year-old Rettie cared for the family. She hoped the Ragamuffin Parade would happen so she could collect pennies for Thanksgiving food. Influenza closed schools and stopped large gatherings, but the parade was held after the war ended and the sickness became weaker. Rettie worked hard, washed rags, cleaned the building, taught the children, and gave Mama Nurse Pauline’s medicine. Mama slowly got better. On November 11, 1918, the family heard that the war was over, and Papa would come home. On Thanksgiving, Rettie marched in the parade and joined the penny scramble. She used her pennies to buy five apples and a small orange pumpkin. Her family shared them with their cabbage dinner.

summaries.summary: In winter, Abuela leaves her sunny home between two rivers and moves in with Mia, Mami, and Papi. Abuela sleeps beside Mia, but they cannot understand each other because Mia speaks little Spanish and Abuela speaks little English. They walk to the park, but have few words to share. Mia remembers how her class helped Kim learn English, so she teaches Abuela words while they make empanadas. They practice with word cards, but communication is still hard. One day, Mia and Mami see a colorful parrot in a pet-shop window. Mia chooses it for Abuela, because it reminds her of the parrot at her old home. They name him Mango. Abuela teaches Mango Spanish words, and Mia teaches them English. With daily practice, all three learn more. Abuela talks with neighbors and tells Mia stories about Abuelo. Mia shows Abuela her art, and they understand each other better. At night, they say, “Hasta mañana” and “Good night,” then fall asleep.

They went to a winter festival, and Katya soon became Sergey’s friend. She loved seeing him every day, but remembered the warning and tried to leave. She was still unhappy, so she returned. One night, she made a huge snowstorm to freeze her heart. During the storm, Sergey disappeared while searching for a sheep. Katya joined the search. She called herself Katya and enjoyed the winter festival with him. Katya and Sergey became friends, and she soon loved him. Afraid of dying, she tried to freeze her heart with a snowstorm. During the storm, Sergey disappeared while searching for a sheep. Katya joined the search and found him unconscious under the melting snow. Her love made her heart warm, and the snow melted. Mother Spring appeared and explained that Katya was now human. She would grow old and die like other people. Katya helped Sergey stand, and they walked together into the warm spring sunshine.

In a town, a princess promised marriage and half the kingdom to anyone who could answer her question, ask one she could not answer, and catch her bird. The drummer used the dark cap and feather to follow the princess to a one-eyed witch’s steel castle. He heard the question and answered it. King Stork helped him ask a question the princess could not answer. Then the drummer caught the one-eyed raven, which was really the witch, in a net. The princess had to marry him. King Stork warned that she was still a witch. After the wedding, the drummer poured milk on her and held her with a hazel switch. She changed into a cat, a wolf, and a snake, then became herself and promised to be good.

video_title: Ruth Law Thrills a Nation STORY

summaries.summary: On November 19, Ruth Law tried to fly from Chicago to New York City in one day, something no one had done before. Before dawn, she put on many warm clothes and went to her plane at Grant Park. Mechanics added a special windshield and an extra gas tank, but removed the lights because the heavy plane had to reach New York before dark. At 7:20, Ruth took off in strong wind. She followed maps attached to her leg and flew for nearly six hours. Near Hornell, the engine stopped because the fuel was gone. Ruth landed safely after flying 590 miles, setting a record. After refueling, she flew on. In Binghamton, Ruth landed before dark because she could not read her instruments. She stayed with kind strangers. The next morning, she flew to New York City, where an army general, a band, and crowds greeted her as a heroine. President Woodrow Wilson praised her, and people celebrated her record.

video_title: The Lotus Seed STORY

summaries.summary: Long ago, Grandmother saw the emperor cry when he lost his Golden Dragon throne. She took a seed from a Lotus pod in the Imperial Garden and hid it under the family altar. She carried it for good luck when she married and kept it when her husband went to war and she raised her children alone. When bombs fell, her family fled Vietnam in a crowded boat. They left their mountains behind and came to America. There, the family worked hard and lived together in one big house. Last summer, Grandmother’s little brother found the seed and planted it near the onion patch. Grandmother cried when he forgot where it was. In spring, a beautiful pink Lotus grew from the mud. Grandmother called it the Flower of Life and hope. When its pod dried, she gave each person a seed. The narrator wrapped one in silk to remember Grandmother and share her story with future children.

video_title: And Still the Turtle Watched STORY

summaries.summary: Long ago, an old man carved a turtle from a large rock at the Delaware people’s summer lodge. He said the turtle would be the eyes of Manitou, watch over the people, and speak to Manitou. Every summer, children came to greet him. The turtle watched the seasons change, and he was happiest when children and their children visited. As time passed, fewer children came. Then strangers arrived. They cut down the forest, made the river water brown, and covered the night with lights. The turtle became sad. One day, boys came near him. He thought they had returned to see him, but they sprayed paint on his eyes and ears. He could not see or hear. Many years later, a man found the painted rock. He brought workmen, who moved the turtle to a botanical garden and scrubbed away the paint. His eyes and ears cleared. Now children visit him, and he will speak of them to Manitou.

Andro asks Ty to bring a washboard, two wooden spoons, a tin pail, and a comb. Ty gets them from his family, but his friends laugh and do not believe Andro will come. At sundown, Ty waits under a street lamp. Andro finally arrives and uses tissue paper, the comb, pail, spoons, washboard, and his peg leg to make music while dancing. The townspeople clap, dance, and shout, “More!” Andro lets Ty and his friends play too, then quietly slips away into the night.

video_title: Dearly, Nearly, Insincerely Read Aloud

summaries.summary: The poem teaches what an adverb is. Adverbs tell when, where, how, how often, or how much something happens. They often describe verbs, as in “quickly do your homework,” “patiently plant peas,” and “slowly he ate.” Some adverbs tell manner, such as slowly, quietly, and sharply. Others tell frequency, such as seldom, always, never, sometimes, and usually. Adverbs can also tell time and place, like yesterday and over there, or order, like first and next. They can show amount with words such as extremely, somewhat, and hardly. Adverbs may describe other adverbs and adjectives, as in “quite nicely,” “very precisely,” and “really blue.” Many adverbs end in -ly, including dearly, bravely, brightly, and uniquely. The poem explains that the adjective good has the adverb well: good describes a day, while well tells how someone felt. It ends by asking, “So what is an adverb? Do you know?”

video_title: Dearly, Nearly, Insincerely Read Aloud

summaries.summary: The poem explains what an adverb is and how it works. Adverbs describe verbs by telling when or how something happens, as in “quickly,” “patiently,” or “lightly.” Many adverbs end in -ly, such as “viciously” and “sly,” and they add detail to sentences. Adverbs of manner tell how an action happens, while frequency adverbs tell how often, using words such as “seldom,” “always,” “never,” “sometimes,” and “usually.” Other adverbs tell how much, including “extremely,” “somewhat,” and “hardly.” The poem also shows that adverbs can tell time, place, and order, with words like “yesterday,” “over there,” “first,” and “next.” They can modify verbs, adjectives, and other adverbs, as in “sang quite nicely” and “really blue.” Finally, the poem explains that “good” is an adjective, while “well” is its adverb, and ends by asking whether the reader now knows what an adverb is.

summaries.summary: Thomas Edison was an inventor who thought of new ideas. He was born in 1847 and asked many questions. After a teacher said he was not bright, his mother, Mrs. Edison, taught him at home. Thomas read many books and made a science lab in the basement, where he mixed and fixed things. At age twelve, he worked on a train and built another lab there. Later, he fixed a broken machine, invented a new one, and used the money to open a large lab. At Menllo Park, Thomas and his helpers made useful inventions, including a copy machine, a device that made telephone sounds louder, and the phonograph, which recorded and played sound. Thomas then worked on an electric light. Many tries failed, but a soot-covered sewing thread glowed inside a glass bulb for hours. On New Year’s Eve in 1879, he switched on many lights at Menllo Park. His electric light bulb helped light the world.

summaries.summary: Little Black Ant lives in a busy ant City under a Sandy Hill on Park Street. After caring for the queens and young ants, she is old enough to find food. She discovers a dead caterpillar but cannot move it, so she leaves a scent Trail. Her nestmates follow it, cut up the caterpillar, and carry the pieces home. The ants share the food with the queen, babies, and workers. They also protect the caterpillar from a large carpenter ant by using their stings and jaws. Later, Little Black Ant gathers honeydew from aphids on a rose bush. A blue jay carries her away in a gum wrapper, and she becomes lost. The next day, she smells her nestmates on their way to a neighborhood picnic. She joins them and helps carry cookie crumbs home. At summer’s end, young Queens fly away to start colonies. Little Black Ant helps close the nest and sleeps through winter. In spring, she will search for food again.

video_title: The Wonder of Wolves Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Wolves are not always fierce animals. They are the ancestors of dogs. Gray wolves live in North America, and timberwolves live in dark forests, where their coats help them hide. Tundra wolves have thick white fur that keeps them warm and helps them hide in snow. In late winter, a mother wolf digs a dry den near water for her pups. The wolf family, called a pack, stays nearby to protect them. Newborn pups cannot see or hear, but by three weeks they can explore outside. Pack members watch them while their mother hunts. At about three months, the pups live with the whole pack. A male and female usually lead the pack, and the others obey them. Wolves use their strong sense of smell and teamwork to track prey, sometimes running forty miles. After eating, they rest and return for the bones. Wolves use whimpers, woofs, and howls to communicate and are important to nature.

video_title: Who Eats What? Coral Reef Food Chains Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Coral reefs are diverse places in warm, shallow ocean water. They cover less than 0.2 percent of the ocean floor, but almost one-third of ocean plants and animals live there. A tiny coral polyp sticks to a rock, builds a hard skeleton, and makes more polyps. Their skeletons join together to form a reef. Reefs grow very slowly, less than one inch each year. They are found near East Africa, South India, Australia, Florida, Brazil, and the Caribbean. Plants such as plankton and seagrass use sunlight to make food. Fish and green sea turtles eat the plants. Larger fish, octopuses, and sharks eat animals. Sharks are top predators. Reefs give animals places to hide. When an animal dies, bacteria break down its body and return nutrients to the sea floor. For example, seagrass feeds fish, an octopus eats the fish, and bacteria break down the octopus. The Great Barrier Reef is in Australia and is the largest reef.

video_title: Who Eats What? Coral Reef Food Chains Read Aloud

summaries.summary: Coral reefs are beautiful, diverse places found in warm, shallow ocean waters. They cover less than 0.2 percent of the ocean floor, but nearly one-third of ocean plants and animals live there, so reefs are called the “rainforest of the sea.” A reef begins when one coral polyp attaches to a rock, builds a hard skeleton, and splits into many polyps. Their skeletons join together over many years, growing less than an inch each year. Reefs are found near East Africa, south India, Australia, Florida, Brazil, and the Caribbean. In the coral reef food chain, plant plankton and seagrass use sunlight to make food. Fish and green sea turtles eat these plants. Larger fish, octopuses, and sharks eat other animals. Reefs also give animals cover from predators. When animals die, bacteria break down their bodies and return nutrients to the sea floor. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia is the world’s largest reef. One food chain can be seagrass, fish, octopus, and bacteria; another can be plankton, sea sponge, fish, eel, and bacteria.

video_title: Straight and Curvy, Meek and Nervy. A Book About Antonyms Read Aloud

summaries.summary: The story teaches about antonyms, which are words with opposite meanings. It gives many examples: sleep and wake, give and take, wet and dry, sell and buy, stand and sit, and strong and weak. Antonyms help people say exactly what they mean. The story compares quiet birds with noisy birds, serious with silly, and a flat road with a hilly road. It also shows that adding word parts such as in, non, dis, anti, ill, or ir can make an opposite word. Examples include mispronounce, mistrust, misspelled, mismatched, anti-social, anti-freeze, irregular, and illogical. More opposite pairs include out and in, neat and messy, shallow and deep, loose and tight, rainy and sunny, healthy and sick, quick and sluggish, kind and mean, plump and thin, spotless and dirty, real and fake, and day and night. Antonyms show differences, such as wrong and right, and brighten English.

summaries.summary: The narrator, “I am the Lord your God,” describes being with African Americans in their struggle for freedom. The narrator heard Africans sing “Kumbaya” on ships, rang church bells for Richard Allen, Absalon Jones, and James Varick, and guided Harriet Tubman and others escaping slavery. The narrator beat the drum for the U.S. Colored Troops in the Civil War and lit colleges built by Booker T. Washington and Mary McLeod Bethune. The narrator was a microphone for Marion Anderson at the Lincoln Memorial and supported Rosa Parks, the Montgomery bus boycott, freedom rides, sit-ins, and Emmett Till’s grieving mother. The narrator shared Martin Luther King Jr.’s dream and helped injured marchers in Selma. The narrator held Ruby Bridges’s hand and supported Fannie Lou Hamer’s fight for voting rights. The narrator was the Bible beneath Barack Obama’s hand when he became president and remains with people seeking justice and freedom.

video_title: Martin's Big Words: The Life of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. | READ ALOUD

summaries.summary: Martin saw “white only” signs in his hometown and felt sad. His mother told him he was as good as anyone. At church, Martin heard his father preach and read the Bible. He grew up to become a minister. He learned from Gandhi and taught that love could drive out hate. In 1955, Rosa Parks was arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat. Black citizens stopped riding buses for 381 days. Martin walked, talked, sang, and prayed with them until they could sit anywhere. For ten years, Black Americans marched for equal rights. Some were jailed or hurt, but Martin told them not to fight with fists. His home was bombed, and people threatened him, but the marches continued. Lawmakers ended segregation, and the “white only” signs came down. Martin won the 1964 Nobel Peace Prize. In 1968, he was shot and died in Memphis while helping striking garbage collectors. His big words are alive today.

At home, Mama tells him to be quiet because Benji has had a bad day at preschool and is hiding in his box. Samuel feels upset because everyone takes care of Benji, but no one notices him. He tries to play karate, then spills milk while making cereal. Samuel cries, but Benji sees him. Benji comes out, spreads his big blue blanket, and wraps Samuel up like a burrito. He says, “You’re my little burrito.” Samuel lets Benji into the blanket and says, “You’re my little brother.” Mama finds them, and the brothers stay together. Good or bad, they will be okay side by side.

Samuel tries to make cereal, spills the milk, and cries angry, sad, shivery tears. Benji notices. He comes out, spreads his blanket, and rolls Samuel up tightly. Benji calls him, “You’re my little burrito.” Samuel lets Benji inside and calls him his little brother. Mama joins them. The brothers know they will be okay together, whether days are good or bad.

video_title: A rose, a bridge and a wild black horse

summaries.summary: A girl asks her mother to guess what she will do when she grows up. She says she will break pretty geodes open with her bare hands, capture and tame a wild black horse, climb a mountain for a stone, and swim across an ocean for a shell. She will do all her mother’s arithmetic, although she wishes someone would do her math too. She will win a race in the fastest car and take her mother for a ride at 100 miles an hour. She will fight and defeat anyone her mother does not like. She will build a huge bridge and a castle for her mother, pick the pinkest rose for her to smell, and leave her a friend while she explores the world. The story says these are many wonderful things, but a mother wants her child’s love, hugs, cuddles, and company most of all.

video_title: Hockey Hero

summaries.summary: Grace and her friend Miles put on their skates and join the Polar Bears for practice. Coach has them practice skating, racing, and shooting. Grace is a fast, skilled skater, but she misses the net five times. She feels sad and thinks about quitting because the big game is coming. Miles tells her the team needs her and offers to help her shoot if she helps him skate faster. After practice each day, Grace helps Miles push harder and gain speed. Miles teaches Grace to slow down, watch the net, and keep her eyes open. Soon, she scores a practice goal and decides to keep playing. During the game against the Dragons, Miles hurts his ankle, so Grace enters the game. She scores twice by slowing down, using her speed, and shooting carefully. With the game tied and one minute left, Grace scores again. The Polar Bears win three to two. Miles calls her a hockey hero and celebrates her hat trick.

video_title: Shine

summaries.summary: Little Hosy is a sea star who lives in the ocean. Each night, she looks at the stars in the sky and wishes she could be there and shine. In the daytime, the tide carries her back into the water. Hosy sees coral, an octopus, fish, crabs, snails, minnows, turtles, and a blue whale, but she wants to live in the sky. She says, “A star stuck in the sea!” Her friends try to cheer her, but she swims down to the dark bottom. There, she wishes for a star under the sea. A glowing anglerfish comes near, and Hosy learns that it shines because it is happy. The anglerfish says happiness is found in the heart. Hosy understands that happiness comes from inside. She swims upward to her friends and sees the ocean as colorful, magnificent, and full of possibilities. Looking into her happy heart, she shines too.

Her friends try to cheer her, but she swims down to the dark, murky bottom. There she sees what looks like a star and wishes for a star under the sea. The glowing shape is an anglerfish, who explains that she shines because she is happy wherever she is. Happiness, she says, comes from inside, pointing to her heart. Hosy understands and swims upward. Seeing her colorful world and wonderful friends in a new way, she realizes there are exciting possibilities in the sea. She looks into her happy heart and shines.

video_title: 'Carla's Glasses' read by Nicola Coughlan

summaries.summary: Ms. Pimento tells the class about Vision Screening Day. Carla hopes she will need glasses, so she can be different. Each day, she makes new pretend glasses: purple pipe-cleaner frames, craft-stick frames, paper star frames, glittery Sparkle Cats, and more. At the screening, Carla reads most of the eye chart, but she does not need glasses. Buster learns that he probably does need them. At Dr. Ollie’s Eyewear, Buster has an eye exam and chooses frames. He feels worried because he likes to blend in, and glasses will make everyone notice him. Carla wants to help. At home, she cuts, glues, bends, shapes, and paints many pretend glasses. The next morning, she gives them to Ms. Pimento. When Buster enters class wearing his new glasses, everyone is wearing a different pair made by Carla. Buster laughs and feels better because he blends in with the class.

video_title: 'Getting to Know Ruben Plotnick' read by Zach Braff

summaries.summary: Ruben Plotnick, called “The Plotnick,” is a funny and very smart boy at school. He does silly things, and everyone wants to be his friend. One day, Ruben goes to David’s house to do homework. David worries about meeting Grandma Rosie because she forgets things, calls him “little boy,” and sometimes asks to dance with Grandpa Nate, who died. Grandma sits in the kitchen while Ruben makes chocolate milk by crumbling cookies into milk and blowing bubbles through a straw. Grandma asks Nate to waltz and looks at Ruben. David tries to dance with her, but she keeps asking. Ruben climbs out of the sink and says she wants to dance with him. He puts his arm around Grandma Rosie, and they waltz around the kitchen. Ruben does not make fun of her or copy her voice. Grandma is happy, and David learns that Ruben is kind and different from how he seems at school.

David worries that Ruben will laugh at Grandma Rosie, who forgets things, mixes things up, and sometimes argues with Grandpa Nate, who died years ago. Grandma Rosie loves to sing, play checkers, eat chocolate cookies, and dance. In the kitchen, Ruben makes chocolate milk by crumbling cookies into plain milk and blows bubbles through a straw. Grandma calls him “little boy.” Then she asks Nate to waltz. David tries to dance with her, but she keeps looking at Ruben. Ruben climbs out of the sink, takes Grandma’s hand, and waltzes with her around the kitchen. He does not make fun of her or copy her voice. Grandma is happy, and David learns that Ruben is kind and different from the class clown he knows at school.

She loves dancing and often calls, “Nate, let’s waltz!” At the house, Ruben makes chocolate milk by crumbling cookies into plain milk and blows bubbles while sitting in the kitchen sink. Grandma calls him “little boy,” then asks Nate to dance. When David tries to help her, she refuses and keeps looking at Ruben. Ruben leaves the sink, takes Grandma’s arm, and waltzes with her around the kitchen. He does not imitate or make fun of her. David realizes Ruben is more thoughtful than his school behavior suggested and is glad to know him better.

video_title: 'So Much Slime' read by June Squibb

summaries.summary: Matty’s family loves making slime. Mom explains that slime needs glue, baking soda, and saline, while Dad says pizzazz makes it special. At school, Matty gets permission to demonstrate slime for the class. He uses six bottles of glue, baking soda, and food coloring, but forgets the saline. The mixture spreads into an icky, sticky swamp. Matty’s classmates try pompoms, sand, felt letters, and mixing to fix it, but these ideas make the mess bigger. The school nurse adds prizes, but the swamp remains. Then Owen brings saline from the science lab. When the class squirts it into the mixture, the swamp becomes squishy slime. Everyone kneads it, and the slime picks up the extra mess, making cleanup easy. There is enough slime for everyone. At home, Matty receives a journal with a slime recipe from Principal Stuckey. He makes glow-in-the-dark slime with his parents and learns that help can turn a mistake into something good.

Matty learns that with help from friends, teachers, and family, a messy mistake can be cleaned up and become something good.

video_title: 'The Mess That We Made' read by Kathryn Hahn

summaries.summary: The story begins with a mess in the ocean. Fish swim in the mess, and a seal eats the fish. A net catches the seal. A steel boat dumps the net, while a current rocks the boat and moves through the bay. A green and gray turtle rides the current. Plastic that people throw away traps the turtle. The landfill grows each day and spills plastic into the bay. The people, at work and at play, fill the landfill, so they help make the mess. Then the people decide to save the day. They reduce their waste, recycle plastic, and make the landfill smaller. They rescue the turtle and haul garbage from the bay. They protest the steel boat, collect the nets, and free the seal. The seal can eat fish that swim in the ocean they save.

They protest the boat, collect the nets, and free the seal. The fish can then swim in the ocean they have saved.

video_title: 'Being Frank' read by Bob Odenkirk

summaries.summary: Frank always told the truth. He said Dotty’s freckles looked like the Big Dipper and Carol’s singing sounded shrieky. He told Ms. Zaroma that her breath smelled funny and Principal Wiggins that his toupee looked like a weasel. Frank even told his mother that her wrinkles came from glaring and that she was speeding. The adults and children became upset, although police officers liked his honesty. Frank felt unhappy, so he visited Grandpa Ernest. Grandpa explained that he had told Mrs. Peacock the good part of her flower-covered hat instead of the bad part. When Mr. Pickles asked about his awful relish, Grandpa honestly said it needed more sugar and less pepper, so Mr. Pickles thanked him. Grandpa told Frank to tell the truth in the right way. At the carnival, Frank gave kind, true compliments, and Carol invited him on the Ferris wheel. Later, Frank complimented Mrs. Peacock’s strange hat. He learned that honesty is best served with more sugar and less pepper.

video_title: 'Being Frank' read by Bob Odenkirk

summaries.summary:
Frank told the truth even when his words hurt. He said Dotty’s freckles looked like the Big Dipper and Carol’s singing sounded shrieky. He told Ms. Zaroma about her breath, Principal Wiggins about his toupee, and Mom about her wrinkles and speeding. Everyone became upset, and Carol would not ride the Ferris wheel with him. Frank wondered if honesty was best.

He visited Grandpa Ernest. Grandpa said truth should be served the right way. He praised the good part of Mrs. Peacock’s flower-covered hat. When Mr. Pickles asked about his relish, Grandpa said it needed more sugar and less pepper. Mr. Pickles thanked him because he had asked for the truth.

At the school carnival, Frank used kind, true words. He praised Ms. Zaroma’s jokes, Wiggins’s spins, Dotty’s dots, and Carol’s high notes. Carol invited him on the Ferris wheel. Frank praised Mom’s hair and did not mention her wrinkles. Later, he kindly answered Mrs. Peacock about her hat. Frank still believed honesty was best, with more sugar and less pepper.

video_title: 'Being Frank' read by Bob Odenkirk

summaries.summary: Frank always told the truth, but he often hurt people’s feelings. He said Dotty’s freckles looked like the Big Dipper, Carol’s singing was shrieky, Ms. Zaroma’s breath smelled funny, Principal Wiggins’s toupee looked like a weasel, and his mother had wrinkles and was speeding. Adults and schoolmates became upset, so Frank visited Grandpa Ernest. Grandpa explained that he had not lied to Mrs. Peacock: he praised the purple flower on her enormous hat instead of criticizing the other flowers. When Mr. Pickles asked about his terrible relish, Grandpa honestly said it needed more sugar and less pepper, and Mr. Pickles thanked him. Grandpa told Frank to give people the truth in the right way. At the school carnival, Frank complimented Ms. Zaroma, Mr. Wiggins, Dotty, and Carol, so Carol invited him onto the Ferris wheel. He also wrote a kind poem for his mother. Later, Frank kindly answered Mrs. Peacock’s question about her strange hat. Frank still believed honesty was best, but learned it should be served with more sugar and less pepper.

video_title: 'Memoirs of an Elf' read by Sutton Foster

summaries.summary: On Christmas Eve, Spark, Bobbin, and Nutshell help Santa fly around the world. Spark has the GPS, Bobbin has the toy bag, and Nutshell has the Nice List. They leave at midnight with 24 hours to visit every house. Santa stops to pet dogs, eat cookies and tamales, and play with a train, so Spark worries they will be late. The elves and reindeer help, and they finish with 30 minutes left. At home, they find Tugboat, a dog, hiding in the toy bag. They accidentally took him from his family! Momma Claus tells everyone to fly back. In daylight, they wear disguises and sunglasses. They land near Tugboat’s house and see his family crying. Santa lets Tugboat run home. The family hugs and kisses him, and they are happy again. Santa says, “No Tugboat, no Christmas.” Then everyone flies home and takes an elfie.

The elves realize his family will be sad, so Momma Claus orders everyone back into the sleigh. Though it is daylight, they disguise themselves and fly to Tugboat’s home. The children are crying because Tugboat is missing. Santa tells Tugboat to go, and the dog races through the snow to his family. They hug him happily. Santa says, “No Tugboat, no Christmas,” and they return home.

video_title: 'La nevera de Maddi' leído por Isabella Gomez

summaries.summary: Sofia and Maddie play at the park. Maddie climbs the wall, but Sofia cannot reach the next hold. At home, Sofia learns that Maddie and little Ryan have only bread and milk because their family does not have enough money. Sofia promises not to tell. Sofia’s refrigerator is full, so she tries to bring Maddie food. She packs fish, eggs, and then burritos, but the fish and eggs make a mess in her backpack. Maddie encourages Sofia while they climb. One day, Maddie reaches the top first, then helps Sofia by letting her grab her hand. Sofia reaches the top too. Sofia worries because Maddie’s refrigerator is still nearly empty. She tells her mom, who says she did the right thing. They bring Maddie’s family bags of food, including milk, meat, vegetables, and cheese pizza bombs. Sofia’s mom says a promise is important, but Sofia says Maddie is more important. They remain friends and share a snack.

Sofia says Maddie is more important than the promise, and they remain friends.

video_title: 'The Busy Life of Ernestine Buckmeister' read by Connie Britton

summaries.summary: Ernestine Buckmeister is very busy. Each morning, her parents tell her to enjoy life, but they fill her afternoons with lessons. She sculpts on Mondays, does water ballet on Tuesdays, knits on Wednesdays, plays tuba on Thursdays, yodels on Fridays, practices karate on Saturdays, and does yoga on Sundays. Nanny O’Dear takes her everywhere, saying, “Oh, dear!” when things get mixed up. Ernestine watches Hugo play outside, but she never has time to join him. One day, Hugo’s ball lands in her tuba, and Ernestine wishes she could play. That night, she looks at her busy schedule and gets an idea. The next day, she takes Nanny to a hilltop instead of going to yodeling. They look at clouds, pretend to be tiny bugs, build a twig fort, and make a daisy crown. When Ernestine misses yodeling, her parents search for her at knitting and karate. They then decide to look at water ballet.

video_title: 'The Busy Life of Ernestine Buckmeister' read by Connie Britton

summaries.summary: Each morning, Ernestine’s parents hurried to work, telling her, “Live life to the fullest” and “Make every moment count.” But Ernestine had no time to play with Hugo because her after-school schedule was full. She sculpted, did water ballet, knitted, played tuba, yodeled, practiced karate, and did yoga every week. Nanny O’Dear helped her get to each class, though the busy schedule sometimes caused confusion. Ernestine watched Hugo play whenever she passed his yard. One day, his ball flew over the fence and landed in her tuba. Ernestine wanted to play, but Nanny reminded her about tuba lessons. That night, Ernestine thought about Hugo and made a plan. The next day, she took Nanny to the park instead of going to yodeling or knitting. They lay on a hill, studied clouds, imagined being tiny bugs, built a twig fort, and made a daisy crown. When Ernestine missed class, her parents searched for her. They asked at knitting and karate, then decided to look at water ballet.

video_title: 'The Busy Life of Ernestine Buckmeister' read by Connie Britton
